Energy Compass — states and strategies guide

English · Polski

This guide explains what Energy Compass does, every state its entities can report and the conditions that produce each state, and the six dispatch strategies. It describes release 0.1.45. The mathematical contract behind each rule lives in model and limitations; installation is described in the Installation section, and dashboards in the installation guide.

Energy Compass is advisory. It computes a plan and publishes it as Home Assistant entities. It sends notifications only when you turn them on (see Window notifications), and it writes inverter settings only when you enable the optional Deye controller (off by default), which does so through the Solarman integration; other controllers decide for themselves whether to act on the plan. See Deye inverter controller.

Installation

This section takes you from an empty Home Assistant to the first plan, step by step. You need a running Home Assistant and, for the full benefit, an inverter with a battery; you do not need to know Energy Compass first. Polish households are the main path (PLN, tariff G12, RCE sell price, net billing), and the same steps apply to any other currency and tariff.

Requirements

  • Home Assistant 2026.9.1 or later.
  • scipy, the numerical solver. The integration installs the exact pinned version from its manifest (scipy==1.18.1); you install nothing yourself.
  • Raspberry Pi and other ARM64 hosts work. The tested ARM64 Core/Python/solver combination and representative benchmark results are in runtime validation.

Install the integration

  1. HACS (recommended). In HACS open Custom repositories and add https://github.com/datamindzio/ha-energy-compass as an Integration. Download Energy Compass, then restart Home Assistant.
  2. Manual. Copy this repository's custom_components/energy_compass directory into the custom_components folder of your Home Assistant configuration directory, then restart.

Add the integration

Open Settings → Devices & services → Add integration → Energy Compass. The setup is a short wizard; nothing is saved until its last step.

  1. First form. Fill in Name, Currency (no automatic conversion) and Timezone, choose the optional Preset (provider profile) and set Pv enabled and Battery enabled. The same form offers three optional starting profiles: Prosumer settlement, Polish distribution tariff and Inverter. They pre-fill editable tuning values once, for this new installation only, and never set a price; Polish profiles require currency PLN. See Setup profiles for what each profile fills in.
  2. Detected sources. Energy Compass looks for Solcast, rce_pse, Solarman (Deye) and your Energy dashboard sources by integration identity, not by entity name, and offers them as rows. Keep the ones you want and continue: they are bound and Preview and save opens. Nothing found, or nothing kept, opens the main menu instead. See Detected sources; PV can also use the Energy dashboard solar forecast.
  3. Main menu. Work through the groups you need; each can be revisited later in Configure. - Tariffs → Buy source for the buy price. For Polish G11/G12/G12w/G13 choose Polish tariff schedule, which needs no YAML: pick the operator and group, then a seller offer (or distribution only, or Enter the rates myself) to pre-fill the rates in Tariffs → Fixed rates and transformations, where every value stays editable. Zones, clock, holidays and the pre-filled rates are in Built-in Polish tariffs. - Tariffs → Sell source for the sell price. For Poland choose RCE market price (PSE), which takes the sensor of the rce_pse integration. - Load forecasting holds the numbers behind the household consumption forecast. A new installation starts from the daily estimate you type there (Daily load kwh, 10 kWh/day by default). Recorder history is used once a household load source is bound: keep the Household load history row in Detected sources, or use Sources → Add source → Load. Load forecasting then tunes the history window (Lookback days, Minimum samples, Recency half-life days) and the fallback. - Sources reviews and edits every bound source, including PV; Battery and Hardware capabilities hold the battery limits and the grid import limit. The planning, outlook, performance and presentation groups appear after Show expert settings (see Expert settings).
  4. Preview and save. The preview normalizes the inputs, shows their coverage, units and ages, and solves a bounded base plan before anything is saved. The base plan must be feasible to save. On first setup you also tick the confirmations for the displayed buy source and household load source (a fixed buy rate of zero means free import; the default household estimate is 10 kWh/day), then confirm the save.

To try Energy Compass without any provider entities, create a synthetic setup: name Synthetic, currency EUR, timezone UTC, preset Generic, PV and battery off; the README (English, Polski) lists the remaining values.

After installation

The integration creates one device with the native sensors, binary sensors and the Strategy select described in Entity overview. Right after saving, the Optimizer status sensor reads calculating and turns ready when the first validated plan is published. If it reports invalid_input, timeout or infeasible, see Optimizer status for the reason.

After an update through HACS, restart Home Assistant and reload the browser page (on the mobile app, restart it). The frontend caches the integration's labels; without a reload, new options such as Energy Atlas can show as blank items.

Optional next steps

Each step is independent; the linked section has the details. Options and Configure are the same button on the integration's page in Settings → Devices & services.

  • Deye inverter controller. To let Energy Compass write the plan to a Deye inverter through Solarman, open Options → Deye controller. Off by default; see Enabling the controller.
  • Notifications. In Notification preferences select a phone or notify entity and turn on Notify enabled; Energy Compass then sends the window notifications itself. Try the target with energy_compass.send_test_notification. See Window notifications and Opt-in notifications.
  • Automatic strategy switching. The strategy_switch blueprint picks one dispatch strategy per day. See Automatic strategy switching and Import the strategy switch blueprint.
  • Dashboards and cost card. Ready-made dashboard examples and the cost card are described in Dashboard examples and the Cost card.
  • Energy Atlas. The optional telemetry service is under Configure → Energy Atlas; see Energy Atlas.

How it works

Each calculation proceeds as follows:

  1. Snapshot and validate inputs. Prices, PV forecast, load forecast (from recorder history), battery SOC and daily counters are read and checked for freshness, units and plausibility.
  2. Build the problem. Native tariff slots (typically 15 min) over the planning horizon (24 h by default), hardware limits, SOC bounds, the carried operating-mode commitment and the active strategy bundle.
  3. Solve the base plan. A mixed-integer linear program minimizes cost (plus strategy weights) under energy balance, battery, grid, mode-duration and export/charge-policy constraints. The proven optimum is published; when solve_time_limit_s runs out first, the best validated solution found so far is published instead and marked time_limited with its mip_gap.
  4. Probe consumption. For each display interval, the solver is rerun with 1 kWh of extra load; the cost difference is the incremental cost of one more kWh, which is classified into a consumption level.
  5. Profile flexible loads. Separate solves for 3, 5, 10, 15 and 20 kWh blocks measure how much flexible energy can be scheduled before the price degrades.
  6. Publish. One coherent generation updates all entities; unchanged entities are not rewritten.

Recalculation cadence

  • Periodic: refresh_minutes (default 15, max 60) aligned to the wall clock; the Deye hybrid setup profile pre-fills 60.
  • Input-driven: at most once per minimum_replan_seconds (default 900 s, 0 disables) while a valid plan is retained; SOC counts as changed only after moving soc_trigger_percent (default 5 %) from the value that started the last calculation.
  • Boundaries: at each native settlement boundary the existing plan advances (consumed rows are dropped, mode clocks tick) without a solve.
  • Plan lifetime: a new plan is valid until generated_at + 2 × refresh_minutes, capped by forecast coverage.
  • Grid outage: while the Deye controller reports a grid outage no solve starts, whatever triggers it; when the outage ends a solve starts at once.

Load forecast

The history forecast is a per-hour mean of complete hours of the last lookback_days, in the local timezone, grouped weekday/weekend (group_weekends) and needing minimum_samples hours per bucket. A plain mean follows a level change only as fast as the window turns over: after a 28-day lookback a house that started heating this week is still forecast at mostly last month's level, and the morning is the first to show it.

forecast_half_life_days (Recency half-life days, default 0 = off, range 0-60) weights each sample by 0.5^(age / half-life), with the age counted from the start of the forecast. The result is still a mean, so margins stay in the reserve logic (Peak-period reserve). minimum_samples counts samples, not weight. With 0 the forecast is the plain mean as before.

benchmarks/load_forecast_backtest.py forecasts each day at local midnight from the hours before it and reports MAE and bias (forecast − measured, kWh per hour) for the morning (06-13) and evening (15-22). It takes a Home Assistant recorder (--recorder-db, --statistic-id), a CSV of hours or a synthetic scenario. Measured on the synthetic scenarios (70 days, 28-day lookback, evaluated over the 20 days after a step of the morning level; not the household's own history):

Method Level change: morning MAE / bias Level change: evening MAE Stable house: evening MAE
plain mean 0.390 / −0.387 0.180 0.151
half-life 3 d 0.214 / −0.148 −0.4 % +7.8 %
half-life 5 d 0.250 / −0.212 −3.8 % +2.8 %
half-life 7 d 0.278 / −0.253 −3.8 % +1.2 %
plain × mean of the last 3 d / lookback 0.233 / −0.197 +43 % +8.8 %
plain × mean of the last 7 d / lookback 0.259 / −0.229 +17 % −0.0 %

Evening columns after the first are changes against the plain mean. A half-life of 5 days is the shortest that keeps the evening within 5 % on both scenarios, and recency weighting cuts the morning error by a third; a single level ratio over the whole day (last N days / lookback) moves the evening the wrong way and was not built. The default stays off until the numbers are reproduced on the household's own recorder with the command above; set 5 to turn it on.

Setup profiles (new installations)

Three axes on the first (User) setup form, Prosumer settlement, Polish distribution tariff (buy_tariff) and Inverter, pre-fill editable tuning for a brand-new installation. Each axis is chosen once; all default to Generic or None (no assignments), and picking a profile applies its assignments to the draft immediately. This is revision 4 of the setup profiles; an entry created under an earlier revision keeps its record and is never re-resolved. The pinned values below (0.20, 0.60, 0.13) were measured or backtested on one site — a G12 buy tariff, net-billing RCE sell and a Deye LFP battery — and are a starting point, not a universal default.

Settlement axis:

Profile Currency Pre-fills Basis
generic any none —
pl_net_billing PLN import_penalty_per_kwh 0.20 · terminal_mode value · terminal_value_per_kwh 0.60 · sell_multiplier 1.23 (only with preset pse/pse_solcast or an RCE market price sell source) backtested on one site
pl_net_metering_80 PLN sell_multiplier 0.8 net-metering ratio, installations ≤ 10 kWp
pl_net_metering_70 PLN sell_multiplier 0.7 net-metering ratio, installations > 10 kWp

Polish distribution tariff axis (buy_tariff): the profile only pre-selects Tariffs → Buy source → Polish tariff schedule for the chosen tariff; it assigns no setting and no price, and the rates stay at 0 until you pre-fill or type them. Every catalog profile requires PLN. The Preview line for a tariff profile reads: "Buy source pre-selected by buy_tariff profile: tariff schedule; pick the seller offer in Tariffs → Buy source to pre-fill the rates, or enter them in Tariffs → Values."; picking the offer is a separate step in the flow, not part of the profile.

Profile Currency Effect Basis

Profile Pre-fills Basis

Every pre-filled value stays fully editable and is never re-applied once the entry exists — not by Configure, not by Reconfigure. While a new installation is still being set up, changing the preset on the Installation step re-resolves the settlement profile: the 1.23 sell multiplier is added or dropped to track the preset (or an RCE market price sell source saved in the meantime) unless you have already edited it. Binding a pre-filled key to a helper overrides the pre-fill at save time; the Preview lists that key as edited, naming the helper and its effective value.

Polish settlement and tariff profiles require currency PLN; choosing one with another currency is rejected, on the field that caused it. Setup profiles never set a tariff price (buy_rate, buy_mid_peak_rate, buy_off_peak_rate, buy_distribution_rate, buy_distribution_mid_peak_rate, buy_distribution_off_peak_rate, sell_rate, buy_addition, sell_addition, monthly_charge) and never touch a strategy-owned setting. They never enable the deposit model either: every installation starts with it off.

Sell only PV (limit_export_to_pv) stays on with every settlement profile — a Polish prosumer may only sell energy produced by their own PV — and is turned off either by switching to the max_export strategy or by setting limit_export_to_pv to off directly; the explicit setting persists across strategy changes.

The 1.23 deposit multiplier applies together with a raw-RCE preset (pse, pse_solcast) or a raw-RCE sell source (Tariffs → Sell source → RCE market price (PSE): a forecast with a price floor and every binding in PLN/MWh). New-entry saves re-evaluate it until the installation is created; Configure and Reconfigure never do. With examples/rce-sell-price.yaml, which already applies the floor and the 1.23 factor itself, keep the sell multiplier at 1 (see tariff helper).

Revision 3 adds one rule to this: when the sell source is a forecast entity that already applies its own settlement (a settlement attribute that names a multiplier, as in the sell template of examples/rce-sell-price.yaml), the 1.23 multiplier is not assigned, even with preset pse or pse_solcast, and binding such a source later removes a 1.23 you did not edit. Binding that template through Detected sources also sets the sell multiplier to 1.

Net-metering's sell_multiplier is a one-time copy of the ratio, not a link to the buy price: it is an approximation (the yearly kWh bank and G12 band mismatch are not modelled), and a later edit to the buy price does not update it.

A net-metering installation runs the battery in the inverter's own self-use mode. Set the inverter to self-use (load first, no grid charging, no battery export), keep allow_grid_charge off and allow_battery_export off (both are off by default and stay off with these profiles), and do not enable the Deye controller. Net-metering is not settled per hour: under the Renewable Energy Sources Act (consolidated text Dz.U. 2026 poz. 68, art. 4) fed-in energy is settled against energy drawn at the ratio 1 : 0.8 (1 : 0.7 above 10 kW) and the balance is carried forward for 12 months, so an exported kWh is worth ratio kWh of a later import — nothing once the year's credit covers the year's import — and the fixed part of the bill steps with the annual draw (capacity-fee bands at 500, 1 200 and 2 800 kWh). None of that is a price per hour or lies inside a 24-48 h horizon, so the plan cannot lower the yearly bill. The planner stands down there: no engine, strategy or profile change, and the costs shown (expected_net_cost, consumption_cost, the cost card, tools/replay.py) stay hourly prices — the kWh are exact, the money is an approximation.

Measured on 40 simulated homes (G11 and G12, ratio 0.8, 10 kWh battery, one year re-planned every hour against the same battery in plain self-consumption, valued with the annual bill, ADR-0008): the default plan (cost_min, as the profile ships) has a yearly gain against self-use, bill plus battery wear, of −93…+70 PLN (mean −1; + = cheaper, − = dearer), never lowers the bill by more than 10 PLN, and raises the annual import by +33…+704 kWh. Priced hour by hour, as Home Assistant reports it, the same G12 plan shows a gain of +343 PLN per year that the settlement does not pay. With Allow grid charge on (13 homes) the yearly gain against self-use, bill plus battery wear, is −209…+139 PLN (same sign convention), and the import rises by +897 kWh (median). Limits: simulated homes, one battery size (10 kWh), one year of prices, hourly intervals, G12 zones netted as one mean rate.

Preview shows setup-profile provenance for a profiled new entry: which keys each axis pre-filled, the buy source pre-selected by a buy_tariff profile, any value edited after pre-fill (including a helper-bound key, with the helper's effective value), and settlement notes — Sell only PV off, a sell source that already applies its own settlement multiplier, raw RCE prices not floored at 0 (with the RCE market price shortcut as the fix) or floored while the 1.23 multiplier is missing, or a net-metering sell that no longer tracks buy — shown only for installations that used a setup profile. For a net-metering profile Preview always adds one more note, and a second when Allow grid charge or Allow battery export is on (English only):

  • "Note: net-metering is settled on yearly kWh (an exported kWh takes back 0.8 kWh within 12 months), not on hourly prices: price-driven dispatch does not lower the yearly bill and the costs shown are an hourly approximation. Run the battery in the inverter's own self-use mode and do not let a controller follow this plan." (0.7 on the 70 % profile.)
  • when Allow grid charge or Allow battery export is on, "Note: Allow grid charge is on: under net-metering energy sent through the grid comes back at 0.8 and raises the yearly import; turn it off." (naming the one that is on, or "Allow grid charge and Allow battery export are on").

The selection, together with the setup-profiles revision that resolved it, is stored on the config entry (setup_profiles) and included in diagnostics.

Built-in Polish tariffs

For a Polish household, Tariffs → Buy source → Polish tariff schedule (G11/G12/G12w/G13) replaces the tariff helper YAML (the YAML example stays the fallback). Pick one of thirteen catalog entries; the zones come from the distributor's 2026 tariff. The rates can be pre-filled from the bundled 2026 operator tariffs and seller offers, or typed: Tariffs → Fixed rates and transformations holds Buy rate (G11, or the peak rate), Mid-peak buy rate (G13 only) and Off-peak buy rate (G12/G12w/G13). Every rate the tariff uses must be above zero or the calculation fails closed with a message naming those fields. The price of a slot is rate × multiplier × VAT factor + addition, as for a fixed rate. The schedule needs no entity and does not limit the planning horizon. It requires currency PLN.

Key Operator and group Weekday off-peak (tariff clock) Free days Source
g11 any, G11 none, one rate — —
pge_g12 PGE Dystrybucja, G12 Apr–Sep 15–17 and 22–6; Oct–Mar 13–15 and 22–6 as weekdays tariff 2026 §2.2.6/2.2.8/2.2.11
pge_g12w PGE Dystrybucja, G12w as pge_g12 all day same
tauron_g12 Tauron Dystrybucja, G12 13–15 and 22–6 as weekdays tariff 2026 §2.2.6/2.2.7/2.2.9
tauron_g12w Tauron Dystrybucja, G12w 13–15 and 22–6 all day same
enea_g12 Enea Operator, G12 default 13–15 and 22–6; set per meter by Enea as weekdays tariff extract 2026 §2.2.5/2.2.7/2.2.12
enea_g12w Enea Operator, G12w 21–6 all day same
energa_g12 Energa-Operator, G12 13–15 and 22–6 as weekdays tariff extract 2026 §3.2.5/3.2.6
energa_g12w Energa-Operator, G12w 13–15 and 22–6 all day same
stoen_g12 Stoen Operator, G12 13–15 and 22–6 as weekdays tariff 2026 §2.2.5/2.2.6/2.2.11
stoen_g12w Stoen Operator, G12w 22–6 only all day same
tauron_g13 Tauron Dystrybucja, G13 three zones, see below all day tariff 2026 §2.2.6/2.2.7/2.2.9
enea_g13active Enea Operator, G13active three zones, see below as weekdays tariff extract 2026 §2.2.5/2.2.7/2.2.12

G13 zones. G13 and G13active have three bands, and the band is the price key: peak uses Buy rate, mid-peak Mid-peak buy rate, off-peak Off-peak buy rate (distribution: Distribution rate, Mid-peak distribution rate, Off-peak distribution rate). Tauron G13: mid-peak 7–13 on weekdays; peak 19–22 from April to September and 16–21 from October to March; every other weekday hour is off-peak, and Saturdays, Sundays and statutory holidays are off-peak all day. Enea G13active: Enea's table of restricted and remaining hours per month, with the restricted hours as peak, the remaining hours as mid-peak and the recommended hours as off-peak; there are no free days. The zone names map to bands by Enea's and Tauron's own meaning (Tauron afternoon peak → peak, morning peak → mid-peak, off-peak → off-peak; Enea restricted → peak, remaining → mid-peak, recommended → off-peak), not by price. The three-band rate messages are "tariff schedule needs positive buy rates: set Buy rate, Mid-peak buy rate and Off-peak buy rate" and "distribution with three zones needs all three rates or none". The one- and two-band messages and prices are unchanged.

Free days of G12w are Saturdays, Sundays and statutory holidays (1 and 6 January, Easter Sunday and Monday, 1 and 3 May, Pentecost, Corpus Christi, 15 August, 1 and 11 November, 24 December from 1 February 2025, 25 and 26 December); there are no substitute days. A meter that was not reprogrammed can ignore a newly added holiday such as 24 December; the YAML fallback's off_peak_dates covers that.

Clock. By default the zones follow local time (the Home Assistant time zone): a remote-read meter billed after hourly balancing uses wall-clock zones, so a day can have 23 or 25 local hours. An old non-remote meter keeps a fixed internal clock on winter time (the tariff clause in the sources above); turn on Old non-remote meter on winter time (fixed UTC+1) for it. To choose, compare your invoice's monthly day/night kWh with your hourly import data split by the windows Preview prints; if the summer months are off by about one hour, enable the winter clock. Season and weekday are classified on the date of the chosen clock. Preview prints the clock, today's off-peak windows and, for G12w, the statutory holidays in the horizon.

Enea G12. Enea sets the hours per meter: 8 hours within 22–7 (start 22 or 23) and 2 hours within 13–17 (start 13, 14 or 15). The default is 22 and 13 (Enea FAQ); the extra form asks for both, so check your meter or bill.

Distribution tariff. A buy source that is not a tariff schedule (a fixed rate, an entity, or a dynamic energy price from a forecast) can still take the distributor's zones: Tariffs → Buy source → Distribution tariff (zones for the distribution rates) (currency PLN) offers the same catalog, winter-clock flag and Enea hours, or None (single zone). The zones apply to the two distribution rates of the deposit model (buy_distribution_rate, buy_distribution_off_peak_rate, and buy_distribution_mid_peak_rate for the G13 keys, which give three zones); their band edges become interval boundaries for the planner, as for a schedule. They do not change the buy source. A schedule source keeps its own zones, so choosing a tariff schedule drops a stored distribution tariff. Preview shows both parts of the first interval's buy price, the energy part and the distribution part. The buy row of Sources → Review and edit sources shows the distribution mode, the zones and the rate per zone.

RCE sell price. Tariffs → Sell source → RCE market price (PSE) saves the sensor of the rce_pse integration (attribute prices, value rce_pln, end dtime, PLN/MWh, 15 minutes) as a forecast source with a price floor of 0: the raw value is floored at 0 per kWh before the multiplier, VAT and addition (max(RCE, 0) × 1.23 with the net-billing multiplier). The floor is visible in Preview and is dropped when the source is switched away from forecast or edited so that it is no longer a raw PLN/MWh RCE source. For a new installation, the PL net-billing profile then assigns the 1.23 multiplier; in Configure and Reconfigure set the sell multiplier yourself. Without the rce_pse integration use examples/rce-sell-price.yaml.

Pre-filled rates

Instead of typing every rate, let the integration compute them from the 2026 operator tariffs and seller offers it bundles (custom_components/energy_compass/sources/tariff_rates.json, regenerated by the maintainer once a year; it is read once at start-up, so the flow needs no network). Reached from Tariffs → Buy source → Polish tariff schedule in a new entry, Configure and Reconfigure alike:

  1. Tariff. Pick the catalog entry (and, for Enea G12/G12w, the hours) as before.
  2. Distribution operator. Asked only for G11, which is the same tariff at every operator while its distribution charges differ: PGE, Tauron, Enea, Energa or Stoen. Every other key already names its operator.
  3. Seller offer. The seller's default tariff (URE) and fixed-price offers priced for every zone of the group, Distribution only (I enter the seller's energy price) or Enter the rates myself. The step shows the tariff year, its validity and the date the rates are as of. In the bundled data, Enea G13active has no offer priced for all three zones, so it offers distribution only or manual entry.
  4. Your connection and billing (offer and distribution only): Connection (single or three phases), Billing period (monthly, or every 2, 3, 6 or 12 months, as the operator publishes) and Yearly consumption band (up to 500 kWh/year … above 2800 kWh/year), which selects the capacity and transitional fees. The defaults are the stored choice, otherwise a single phase, monthly billing and the band up to 2800 kWh/year.
  5. Fixed rates and transformations opens with the computed values in place and a line naming the source; every value stays editable and nothing is written back later.

Enter the rates myself saves the schedule as before, with no pre-filling. Choosing an offer writes these settings (all net of VAT, with buy_apply_vat on and VAT added by the price formula):

Setting Value
buy_rate, buy_mid_peak_rate, buy_off_peak_rate the offer's energy price of the zone plus the excise of 0.005 PLN/kWh; a band the tariff does not have is 0 (G11 writes buy_off_peak_rate 0)
buy_distribution_rate, buy_distribution_mid_peak_rate, buy_distribution_off_peak_rate the operator's variable rate of the zone + quality + RES + cogeneration fee per kWh; a band the tariff does not have is 0
buy_distribution_mode, buy_multiplier, buy_addition, buy_apply_vat added, 1, 0, on
vat_percent 23, only when sell_apply_vat (Sell apply vat) is off and vat_percent is not bound to a helper; otherwise it is kept and Preview adds "Note: VAT is 8 % (shared with the sell side); the offer assumes 23 %." (the first number is your value)
monthly_charge (fixed fee for the phases + subscription for the billing period + capacity fee + transitional fee for the band + the seller's trade fee) × (1 + vat_percent / 100 when buy_apply_vat is on), rounded to 0.01 PLN. Reporting only

The excise sits in the energy rate because the deposit model's energy part is the buy price minus the distribution part. A price computed this way equals the calculator's price, (energy + excise + distribution) × (1 + VAT), to within 0.001 PLN/kWh.

Distribution only writes the distribution rates, mode, VAT and monthly charge (without a trade fee) and sets the energy rates to 0, and is offered for groups that have offers too. The calculation then fails closed with the positivity message until you type the seller's net energy price plus the excise for each zone: use it when your seller is not in the bundled list.

What is recorded. The schedule keeps the provenance (operator, offer, tariff year, validity, date of the rates, phases, billing period, consumption band and the computed values); nothing else in the runtime changes, since the pre-filled values are ordinary settings. Binding a pre-filled key to a helper afterwards still overrides it, and pre-filling in turn removes the entity binding (helper) of every rate setting it writes (the values step lists them as "Helper bindings removed for: …"; vat_percent is never unbound): a bound helper does not silently win over the offer. The tariff helper YAML stays useful for what the catalog and the bundled offers do not cover: another operator or group, a seller that is not listed, custom dates.

Preview prints "Rates pre-filled from seller: offer (operator tariff year, valid from–to, as of date)" (for distribution only: "Distribution rates pre-filled from the operator tariff year (…); energy rates are 0"), then "; N values edited since" when you changed any of them. Two notes can follow, and neither changes a value: after the end of validity, "the pre-filled rates are out of date (the 2026 tariff ended 2026-12-31); values are unchanged — pick the offer again or edit Tariffs → Values", and when the bundled data holds a newer tariff year for the operator, "newer rates are bundled (tariff 2027): pick the offer again in Tariffs → Buy source". The offer step warns the same way when the bundled tariff has ended. The bundled rates are one snapshot per year (new URE decisions are published every December, and most offers end on 31 December): a release brings the next one, and the values you saved never change on their own.

Downgrade. An older build ignores the two mid-peak settings and the stored provenance, and a G13 key reads "unknown tariff; reconfigure the buy source" and fails closed rather than pricing two zones. Reconfigure the buy source to a G12 entry before going back to an older release.

Detected sources (new installations)

After the first (User) form of a new installation, Detected sources looks for sources Energy Compass can use, binds the ones you keep and opens Preview: the quick path to a first plan. It never runs in Configure or Reconfigure, never changes the preset or a setup profile, and never touches the buy source (the buy_tariff profile and Tariffs stay the only buy path). Candidates are recognised by integration identity (the integration, the entity's translation key and the Energy dashboard preferences), never by entity id or name, so renamed or localized entities are found too. If nothing is found, or you keep nothing, the main menu opens as before. Every bound source stays editable in Sources.

Energy dashboard first. Energy Compass should read the same data as the Energy dashboard. For every role the dashboard covers (lifetime counters, solar, grid and battery power, battery SOC and the solar forecast) the dashboard's choice ranks first; the integration signals below are the fallback. For power it uses the normalized power sensor the dashboard stores. When both exist and differ, both are offered, the dashboard one is preselected and the line names both. The same entity found twice is offered once.

Controls. A row with one candidate is a single checkbox, ticked (BMS SOC: unticked). A row with several candidates is a drop-down: the preselected candidate, the others in order of preference and Do not bind last. A tie that cannot be resolved offers Do not bind preselected. Among equally ranked candidates the single Deye Solarman config entry breaks the tie, for example the dashboard's two grid meters resolve to the inverter's counter.

Row Candidates in order of preference
pv the Energy dashboard solar forecast (solar_forecast, all its integrations added together); Solcast solcast_solar total sensors for today and tomorrow (total_kwh_forecast_today, total_kwh_forecast_tomorrow, attribute detailedForecast)
sell the Energy Compass sell template (template: unique id starting energy_compass_, a settlement attribute naming a multiplier, and prices); rce_pse for today and tomorrow (rce_pse_today_price, rce_pse_tomorrow_price)
load solarman lifetime household consumption (total_load_consumption) as a recorder statistic
soc the dashboard battery SOC; an external SOC template (template, device class battery, unit %); solarman battery
bms_soc solarman battery attribute BMS SOC; the one enabled BMS pack sensor (battery_N); never preselected
soc_estimator one Solarman Deye config entry with total_battery_charge, total_battery_discharge, battery_voltage and battery_current (and battery_power when present); never preselected; see Counter SOC estimator
battery_power the dashboard battery power; battery_power
pv_power the dashboard solar power; pv_power
load_power solarman load_power; used only for Energy Atlas telemetry, never by the load forecast or the optimizer
grid_import_power, grid_export_power the dashboard grid power (sign +1 for import, −1 for export); grid_power with the same signs
pv_energy the dashboard solar energy; total_production
grid_import_energy the dashboard grid import; total_energy_import
grid_export_energy the dashboard grid export; total_energy_export
pv_energy_today today_production
grid_export_energy_today today_energy_export
  • Solarman. Only config entries with at least one device from manufacturer Deye count. The inverter and its BMS packs are devices of one config entry. With several Deye entries every Solarman row has several candidates and no default. The sign conventions (battery + is discharge, grid + is import) were verified on one Deye profile only; the offered value is shown so you can check it.
  • Validation. Each candidate is checked with the parsers Preview uses, on the exact binding that would be stored. Forecasts must parse (tomorrow may be unpublished); counters and power need a numeric state in W, kW, Wh or kWh; a SOC must be a finite value from 0 to 100 (a state SOC needs unit %); a load statistic needs a cumulative state class and kWh or Wh. An unusable candidate is not offered; the notes list it with the reason.
  • Sell template. Binding it sets the sell multiplier to 1, because the template already applies its floor and multiplier. Setup profiles then do not add 1.23 again (see Setup profiles). A stale template is not offered.
  • rce_pse. The sensor must report PLN/MWh (the integration default); the PLN/kWh price unit option is rejected here and in Tariffs → Sell source → RCE market price (PSE), because it would price energy a thousand times too low.
  • Solcast. detailedForecast exists only while the option Include detailed forecast half-hourly is on. The day 3–7 sensors, the hourly detail and the rooftop-site sensors are never used.
  • BMS SOC. It is offered unticked. With imbalanced battery cells the BMS SOC and the battery SOC can differ by more than Battery → Soc disagreement percent (default 5 %), and then every plan is blocked. Tick it only if both agree over a full day.
  • Counter estimator. It is offered unticked next to the BMS row, as Counter estimator (recommended when the BMS SOC is unreliable), when exactly one Solarman Deye config entry has the four sources. Ticking it replaces the soc and bms_soc rows (a ticked BMS SOC moves to the estimator as a comparison reading) and opens its settings before Preview (see Counter SOC estimator). The BMS SOC can be wrong even at 100 %, which is the case the estimator is for.
  • Gates. sell appears only with currency PLN. With PV off there are no pv, pv_power or pv_energy rows; with the battery off no soc, bms_soc, soc_estimator or battery_power rows. The two daily counters are never gated.
  • Stored age limits of the measurements: 3600 s for battery_power, load_power, grid_import_power and grid_export_power; 86400 s for pv_power, the lifetime counters, the battery charge and discharge energy counters and the daily counters (a constant 0 W at night never updates the state).
  • Never detected: buy; throughput_today (to use daily_cycles provide one entity with the AC-side charge plus discharge since midnight, see source requirements); battery_energy, battery_charge_power, battery_discharge_power, battery_charge_energy and battery_discharge_energy (the optional measured calibration counters); and helpers.

Preview then shows the usual acknowledgements for a new entry. Its Back to the main menu checkbox leaves Preview without validating or saving anything. The matching reference tables are in source requirements.

Energy dashboard solar forecast

Sources → Add source → PV → Energy dashboard solar forecast (mode solar_forecast) reads the same solar forecast as the Energy dashboard, from every integration with an Energy solar-forecast platform (Solcast, Forecast.Solar, Open-Meteo and others). Pick one or more loaded integrations; their forecasts are added, as the dashboard adds them. The form defaults to the integrations in the dashboard's solar settings. Detected sources offers the same mode first when the dashboard has a forecast.

  • Hourly dashboard rule. Every value is Wh in the local hour that contains its key; values in one hour are summed. The plan sees hourly energy from the current hour to the last hour with a key, up to 49 hours ahead; keys older than two days are ignored.
  • Night hours that the provider omits count as 0 Wh. A gap inside the day is also 0, so a provider gap makes the plan more conservative.
  • Provider notes. Solcast's platform uses the forecast type chosen in its options (key_estimate, for example the 10th percentile) in 30-minute steps, while the Solcast sensor mode reads pv_estimate. Forecast.Solar reports irregular keys; Energy Compass reads them as the dashboard does.
  • No age check. wh_hours carries no publication time. A forecast update is picked up at the next recalculation (scheduled or event-triggered), not by itself.
  • Failures act like a missing entity: an integration that is missing, not loaded, without a platform or without data makes the inputs invalid with a message naming its domain.
  • No mixing. Entity forecast arrays and Energy dashboard forecasts cannot be combined (both typically come from the same provider, so the energy would be counted twice). Saving one removes the other. Turning PV off in Installation clears both.

Preview adds a line PV source: Energy dashboard solar forecast … for this mode.

Counter SOC estimator

Some packs report a BMS SOC that is wrong even at 100 % (imbalanced cells, a BMS that re-anchors on its own). The counter SOC estimator is a second way to get the battery SOC: instead of reading an SOC entity, Energy Compass computes it inside the integration from the battery's lifetime charge and discharge energy counters. Choose it under Configure → Battery SOC source (sources.soc_mode = counter_estimator); the default stays Entity, the SOC source bound in Sources. The estimator then replaces the SOC and BMS SOC sources for the planner, for the LFP balance and for the native Deye controller. The BMS SOC is not trusted anywhere: there is no BMS-based anchor or fallback, and a BMS SOC source, if you add one in the expert settings, is only shown beside the estimate for comparison.

The arithmetic. The estimator carries an anchor, a known energy above the pack's 0 % point at known counter values, and adds what the counters have moved since:

E = anchor energy − (discharge − anchor discharge) + eta × (charge − anchor charge) + pending

E is clamped to 0 … capacity and the SOC is E / capacity. eta is the charge efficiency of the counters (the counters sit at the battery terminals, the plan's efficiencies are AC-side). pending integrates the battery power between two counter steps, so the value moves smoothly although the counters report in coarse steps (a step is integrated for at most 120 s, pending is held within ±2 kWh and restarts at zero whenever a counter changes). A counter that goes down re-anchors at the current energy (anchor kind reset); a rise faster than 100 kW since the counter's previous step (at most one hour back) is ignored as a glitch unless it repeats. The estimate never jumps on its own.

Zero is a voltage. 0 % is the pack voltage you enter as Pack voltage that is 0 % (empty_voltage, in the pack-voltage scale of the voltage sensor, for example the inverter's cutoff). It is a property of your pack, so there is no default and the step refuses to save without it. The capacity is the usable energy between that point and full; it defaults to the battery capacity of the Battery group (an expert override exists) and the planner scales the estimator fraction by the battery capacity, so keep the two equal.

A full pack is a voltage too. A full anchor needs the charge to have reached Pack voltage a charge reaches at full (full_min_voltage, the same scale as the 0 % voltage). It is a property of your pack, so there is no default and the step refuses to save without it (it must also be above the 0 % voltage). A pack reaches this voltage only while charge current flows and relaxes a few volts once the charge stops (one site: 556 V at the stop, 546 V at rest), so a full candidate starts only within 30 minutes of a reading at or above it, and a running one only needs the resting pack to stay at or above 97 % of it; below that it breaks (logged as below_full_voltage). This voltage, not the counters, says the pack is full: counters that have drifted low must not be able to keep a full pack from correcting them.

Anchors: physical evidence only.

Anchor When Effect
full For full_hold_seconds (at least 3600 s, one hour; default 3600 s) without a break, starting within 30 minutes of a pack voltage at or above full_min_voltage and with the pack at or above 97 % of it throughout, and every source it reads (current, voltage, PV, load, grid) reported within the last 60 s: the pack takes (almost) no charge (current within max(1 A, 2 % of the maximum charge current)); charging was possible (the charge current limit is at least 2 A, and the Deye controller is not in HOLD, CURTAIL, BASE or DISCHARGE_GRID; in CHARGE_GRID only with a Grid program below 99 % of its voltage and a grid charge current of 2 A or more; a candidate that already runs also continues in HOLD, see below); and the cause is not lack of sun, shown by measured grid export of at least max(300 W, 5 % of the rated PV power) while the pack takes none (path export). Only where export is impossible or capped (the planner's export cap grid_export_kw is 0, or the export sits within 5 % of it) does the derived surplus count instead (path surplus): PV − load − the charge the pack still takes ≥ 300 W + 10 % of the PV power, because DC PV minus AC load overstates the real surplus by the inverter's conversion losses. Grid charging requested at 2 A or more below its program voltage is the third path (grid). The counters are not consulted: a pack at the full voltage anchors even when they put it far below the capacity, which is exactly what an anchor is for. E = capacity
full_balance In a plan row that is an LFP balance hold (balance_hold), with a Grid program at its (full) voltage: charging that stops at the program voltage, with the same taper, limit, freshness and voltage conditions held for full_hold_seconds. The plan asked for a full pack and the inverter stopped at the full voltage, so the stop is itself the evidence; the controller's own "target reached" does not explain it away here. E = capacity
empty For 60 s, with the same 60 s freshness, and only if the pack voltage is at least half the 0 % voltage (a 0 V reading is a dropout) and, for the discharge case, the current and the battery power agree on discharging (otherwise no anchor, and the refusal is logged once): discharging at 0.5 A or more at no more than 0.1 C with the voltage at or below the 0 % voltage; or the discharge stopped although the house imports at least 300 W from the grid, the discharge current limit is at least 2 A, the controller state is not HOLD or CURTAIL and the voltage is within 1 % above the 0 % voltage. E = 0 (a downward jump: like any recalibration it revokes the plan for about a minute while fresh reports confirm it); the energy since the last full anchor is shown as measured_capacity_kwh (never applied)
reset A counter went down Re-anchors at the current energy
initial / seed First start: the SOC you state, or the anchor of the SOC template you migrate from Shown as unanchored until the first physical anchor

The full anchor needs the charge current limit (the native controller's entity, or the expert source Charge current limit) and the grid power with the PV power (or the load power); the grid path needs the native controller's program and grid-charge entities. Without them it never fires and the estimate stays an unanchored count. Without the native Deye controller (disabled, or the blueprint engine) the dispatch state and the TOU program are invisible to the estimator, so the full rule rests on the measured grid export (or the derived surplus where export is capped or zero) alone: grid charging never anchors, and the options step says so. For the first 14 days after the estimator starts (or is seeded), full candidates are only logged in the full_candidates attribute, unless Anchor on candidates from day one is on, because the hold has never been seen on a real taper. A candidate shows the start, the values, which path held (export, surplus, grid or balance) and its outcome (anchored, or candidate for one not applied) beside energy_before_kwh, the energy the counters gave just before.

Charging stays allowed during the hold. While a full candidate runs (from its first reading until it qualifies or breaks), the native Deye controller does not close the charge path: where the profile would lower or zero the battery charge current (CHARGE_PV and SELF_CONSUME once the SOC reads 100 %, HOLD, the full-pack rule and the CHARGE_GRID stop at 100 %) it keeps the charge current at the charge cap (limited by max_current, max_power_w / V and the current-ceiling hysteresis), and the program direction stays as the profile sets it: nothing is added, grid charging is never opened for it, and HOLD keeps its own Grid program and grid current. Without this a taper that the controller itself cut would end the evidence and the hold would never complete. A candidate also continues while the plan moves to HOLD (a candidate never starts in HOLD): the charge limit in force, at least 2 A, shows that the controller is holding the path open, and in HOLD only the export and surplus paths count, since its Grid program only holds the SOC. Leaving for CURTAIL, BASE or DISCHARGE_GRID, a charge limit under 2 A for more than 120 s (the controller itself writes 0 A for a moment when the program direction changes, which a running candidate lives through; the limit never starts one), or a voltage under the full voltage ends the candidate, and the profile goes back to its own values. The blueprint engine is unchanged and closes the charge path where its profile says so, so the hold may break there.

Staleness. The estimate is stamped with the newest report of the voltage, current and power sources, but never fresher than its counters allow: once the counters are older than their observed update step, taken as 1.5 times the largest of the last five (at least one minute, at most 15; 15 minutes until a step was seen), the estimate is as old as the counters even while power is fresh. After a restart the first step does not integrate the power stored before the downtime.

Never 100 % by guess. Clamping at the top never creates an anchor. A count that reaches the capacity without a full anchor shows 99.9 % with unanchored_top: true; the energy above the capacity is kept (it is not dropped) and shown as excess_kwh, and leaving the top first spends it. 100 % is shown only after a full anchor, until the pack falls 0.1 kWh below the top. While the top is confirmed, charge counted above the capacity is losses and float, not stored energy: the anchor stays a full one from its original time and takes the current counters, so excess_kwh stays 0 and the energy does not carry a phantom surplus into the next discharge. A full anchor is an upward jump and goes through the same rebase as a BMS recalibration (a retained plan for up to 300 s while fresh reports confirm it).

What reads the estimate.

  • Planner. The coordinator reads the estimate through the same validation as an SOC entity (age, range, jump check), stamped with the newest report of the voltage, current and power sources. There is no entity between them, so a template reload or a restart no longer makes the source unavailable.
  • Deye controller. With the estimator on, the native controller's SOC fact is the estimate: the telemetry gate, the Voltage-mode full-pack rule and the reached checks use it. The controller also reads whether a full candidate runs and then keeps charging allowed (see Charging stays allowed during the hold). Capacity mode is not supported with the estimator: in that mode the inverter compares the SOC thresholds of its programs with its own BMS SOC, so a target in the estimator's scale would be wrong. Saving the estimator is refused (the inverter is in Capacity mode) while a native controller is enabled and the inverter's battery operation mode reads Capacity; switch the inverter to Voltage first. While the estimator is the source the controller also treats Capacity as not commissioned, so a later switch of the inverter to Capacity parks it in the base profile (mode_not_commissioned) instead of writing SOC thresholds. Voltage mode is unaffected (its thresholds are voltages). The deprecated blueprint engine keeps its own soc_entity input and is not changed.
  • LFP balance. A balance counts a pack as full only on physical evidence, not at SOC ≥ the threshold: a full or full_balance anchor, or a standing full candidate (one that has held the full hold, also while the first 14 days only log candidates and apply no anchor). A reading the arithmetic pushed to the threshold never credits a balance. A balance row whose Grid program reaches its voltage and tapers is such evidence, so a completed balance is recorded and not planned again every day. The balance hold (balance_hold_minutes) starts counting only once that evidence has held for the full hold, so with the estimator the planner asks for a window of the balance hold plus the full hold (two hours at the defaults). During the first hour the plan shows that window as an ordinary balance row (the controller charges, the tracker is not yet holding); once the candidate qualifies the tracker holds and the remaining minutes of the balance hold are planned from now. A window of the balance hold alone ends before the evidence qualifies and completes nothing.

Diagnostics. The diagnostic sensor sensor.<name>_soc_estimator (SOC estimator, %, device class battery) exists while the estimator is on or in shadow. Its state is recorded; of its attributes only anchor_kind is recorded: energy_kwh, anchor_at, anchor_age_h, throughput_since_anchor_kwh, pending_kwh, unanchored_top, excess_kwh, full_candidate, measured_capacity_kwh, eta_charge, capacity_kwh, mode (counter_estimator or shadow), bms_soc (comparison only), full_candidates (the last 20) and anchors (the last 20). When the throughput since the last anchor exceeds Warn after this many capacities (drift_warn_cycles, 3) times the capacity, the repair issue The SOC estimator has gone a long time without an anchor appears; it only warns, plans are not blocked, and it clears at the next anchor. The diagnostics download has a soc_estimator block with the same detail and no entity ids.

Settings (Configure → Battery SOC source; Expert settings adds the second table):

Field Meaning Default
soc_source entity or counter_estimator entity
charge_counter, discharge_counter lifetime battery energy counters (kWh or Wh) detected on a Solarman Deye device
voltage, current pack voltage and current (current positive while discharging) detected on a Solarman Deye device
empty_voltage the pack voltage that is 0 % required, none
full_min_voltage the pack voltage a charge reaches at full; a full candidate starts only within 30 min of it and runs while the pack rests at or above 97 % of it required, none
initial_soc_percent SOC to start from when there is no stored state or seed 50
eta_charge charge efficiency of the counters the measured battery round trip when calibration has one, else 0.95
full_hold_seconds hold before a full anchor (at least 3600, one hour) 3600
drift_warn_cycles capacities of throughput without an anchor before the repair issue 3
anchor_on_candidates anchor on full candidates inside the first 14 days off
shadow run as diagnostics only beside the bound SOC entity off
seed_from_template start from the anchor of the bound SOC template (only offered when it has the template's anchor attributes) on when offered
Expert field Meaning
capacity_kwh estimator capacity override (default: battery capacity)
power, pv_power battery power (positive while discharging) and PV power; fall back to the measurements of the same name in Sources
grid_power, load_power grid power (positive while importing) and house load; the load is computed from PV, grid and battery power when absent
charge_limit, discharge_limit, grid_charge_current the inverter's current limits; the native controller's entities are used when it runs

power_sign, current_sign, grid_sign 1 or -1 to flip a sensor's sign

Every source is read in the base unit its entity declares (kWh or Wh, W or kW, V, A).

Setup and detection. On a new installation the Detected sources step offers Counter estimator (recommended when the BMS SOC is unreliable) unticked when one Solarman Deye device has the charge and discharge counters, the pack voltage and the pack current. Ticking it replaces the SOC rows and opens the estimator's settings before Preview, where the pack voltage that is 0 % and the lowest pack voltage of a full pack are required.

Migrating from a template estimator. A site that runs a YAML template estimator can move without a jump:

  1. Open Configure → Battery SOC source, keep Entity, tick Shadow run, enter the counters, the voltage, the current and the 0 % voltage, and tick Start from the anchor of the existing SOC template (offered when the bound entity has the attributes anchor_kwh, anchor_charge, anchor_discharge, anchor_kind, anchor_at; pending_kwh is optional). The planner keeps using the template while sensor.<name>_soc_estimator runs beside it.
  2. After at least one day compare them with tools/soc_shadow.py on the recorder history of both entities (or a directory of state dumps as tools/shadow_compare.py reads them). The acceptance is that the energy differs by at most 0.2 kWh in 95 % of the minutes and that no full or empty anchor of one is missing from the other.
  3. Switch Battery SOC source to Counter estimator, then remove the template's YAML block and reload the templates. Reloading templates makes the template SOC unavailable for a moment; the estimator no longer depends on it.

Limits of this version. Detection offers the estimator for Solarman Deye devices only (other inverters: set the sources in the expert group); efficiency and capacity are never learned or changed automatically; the Capacity-mode restriction above applies.

Expert settings

The main menu of Setup, Configure and Reconfigure starts with the common groups only: Installation, Sources, Battery, Hardware capabilities, Battery SOC source (with a battery), Tariffs, Load forecasting and Notification preferences. Show expert settings adds the four expert groups, Planning, Consumption outlook, Performance and input quality and Presentation, and Numeric helper bindings; Hide expert settings hides them again. The view is per flow and is not stored. Hidden settings keep their values and keep working. A script that drives the options flow over REST must post show_expert before it selects a hidden group, otherwise Home Assistant rejects the step.

Saving options

Saving Configure is applied live. The integration adopts the new settings, sources, helpers and tariffs without reloading the entry, so no entity becomes unavailable and the published plan keeps running as a retained plan (plan_retained=true, refreshing=true, optimizer calculating) until the recalculation publishes its replacement. The Deye controller keeps executing that plan and accepts the new one when it is published; it does not fall back to the base profile. Source and helper bindings are re-subscribed at the same time. The entry still reloads, with the previous plan lost until the first new calculation (the controller keeps executing its accepted plan meanwhile), when the save changes which entities exist or how they are named: Periodic LFP balance charge (lfp_balance), Enable flexible energy depth (flexible_load_enabled), Expose costs (expose_costs), Expose windows (expose_windows), turning the counter SOC estimator (or its shadow run) on or off, the installation name or the currency. A running Energy Atlas is refreshed in place (state tracking and site attributes), without a restart of its sink. Reconfigure always reloads.

Buy and sell price now read buy_per_kwh and sell_per_kwh of the plan.intervals row whose [start, end) contains the current time, whatever the price source (fixed, entity, forecast such as RCE or Pstryk, tariff schedule); they are unknown when no row contains now or the plan is neither valid nor refreshing, and need no new plan to follow an interval boundary. Cost sensors (including these two) can be disabled with Presentation → Expose costs, window timestamps with Expose windows, and flexible depth with Consumption outlook → Enable flexible energy depth. Battery balance is disabled by default and enabled with the LFP balance setting; its attributes carry last_completed, next_due, days_overdue, planned_start, planned_end, planned_mode, pv_series, hold_progress_minutes, hold_required_minutes and threshold_percent.

Availability rule

Optimizer status — calculation lifecycle

State EN / PL label When it occurs What stays published
ready Ready / Gotowy The last calculation produced a validated base plan and it was published: proven optimal, or the best solution found within solve_time_limit_s (time_limited: true). The new plan. ready does not guarantee complete reference coverage — check reason.
calculating Calculating / Obliczanie A calculation is queued or running. reason says why: inputs_changed, interval_boundary (periodic refresh due), inputs_recovered, calculating (worker started), soc_rebase_pending (upward SOC jump awaiting confirmation), grid_outage (the grid is out: no solve starts until it is back, see Grid outage), grid_restored (the outage ended, a solve starts at once). The previous plan while it covers now, with refreshing: true (plan_retained: true during an outage). An existing alert stays on; an outage raises none.
invalid_input Invalid input / Niepoprawne dane A required source is missing, unavailable, stale, in wrong units, out of range, SOC disagrees with BMS or jumped, daily counters are from the previous day, settings are invalid; also no_current_interval and expired_inputs when the retained plan no longer covers now. The previous plan while it covers now (plan_retained: true); otherwise nothing.
timeout Timeout / Przekroczony czas The base solve reached solve_time_limit_s (default 10 s) without any feasible solution, or the worker exceeded total_time_limit_s + 1 (reason worker_deadline). Previous plan within coverage.
infeasible Infeasible / Brak rozwiązania The solver proved no plan satisfies every hard constraint (e.g. SOC reserve, terminal rule, a carried mode commitment, Sell only PV deficit, grid limits). Previous plan within coverage.
error Error / Błąd Any other solver failure or unexpected exception; reason holds the solver reason or exception class. Previous plan within coverage.
insufficient_data Insufficient data / Za mało danych Reserved in translations; not emitted by the current coordinator — missing data reports invalid_input. —

Attributes: last_calculation_started_at, calculations_since_load, expired_previous_generated_at, and measured_calibration when calibration counters are bound (see Measured calibration). Diagnostics add calculations_last_hour and calculations_last_24h.

Measured calibration (optional)

Plans carry calibration and capacity_calibration, which stay unvalidated until you set them and say nothing about how far the configured values are from reality. Two read-only diagnostics compare them with your own counters. They never change a plan. A block appears only while its sources are bound; with none bound, measured_calibration is absent from the Optimizer status attributes (excluded from the recorder) and from the integration diagnostics.

Block Sources (Sources → Add source → Measurement) Reports
battery_round_trip battery_charge_energy and battery_discharge_energy: lifetime counters of the energy that passed the battery terminals, kWh or Wh, battery enabled discharge ÷ charge energy over the last 30 days, next to the configured eta_charge × eta_discharge
pv_forecast_accuracy pv_energy: the lifetime PV counter, PV enabled, an entity (not a recorder statistic) real ÷ forecast PV energy over the last 14 days, in total and per local hour of the day
Field Meaning
status ok, or insufficient_data while the window is too short
window_days, covered_hours Rolling window (30 / 14 days) and the full hours that had every value they need
minimum_hours Covered hours needed before the ratio is shown: 168 for the round trip (and at least 1 kWh charged), 24 for PV
charge_kwh, discharge_kwh Round trip: summed counter deltas over the covered hours
measured, configured, difference Round trip: measured ratio (null until ok), eta_charge × eta_discharge and the first minus the second
forecast_kwh, measured_kwh, ratio PV: sums over covered hours and their quotient; ratio is null when the forecast sum is below 0.05 kWh or while status is insufficient_data
by_local_hour PV: keys "00"–"23" (hour of the day in the installation timezone), each with ratio, hours, forecast_kwh and measured_kwh

How it is measured:

  • Hour boundaries. Each counter reading is stamped with the source's own report time and reduced to its value at every full UTC hour by interpolating between consecutive readings. An unchanged counter is exact however long the gap; a moving one across a gap longer than 2 hours gives no value. Energy of an hour is the difference of its two boundaries.
  • Idle counters. A counter that writes its state only when it moves (a template, utility meter or integration helper) does not report while idle. One that has not changed for more than 2 hours is taken to hold its value up to now, as long as its last report is no older than the source's maximum age (24 hours by default; with the age check off, no limit), so its idle hours count. Only that age tells a frozen source from an idle one: past it the hours drop out. Idle hours appear 2 hours late, and a source that holds a steady non-zero rate without writing its state is read as idle.
  • Missing hours, resets and glitches. An hour without both boundaries is skipped, never filled. A counter that goes down is a reset or a glitch: neither the step down nor the segment that recovers from it yields a boundary, so the hours on both sides drop out of both ratios (a counter that restarts after a reset is used again from its second reading). A rise faster than 100 kW (plus 1 kWh) between two readings is rejected the same way, as is an hour delta above 101 kWh, so a single absurd reading costs a few hours and never skews a ratio.
  • Rebinding. Stored counter values belong to the entity, attribute, multiplier and unit they were read from. Binding the role to something else clears that counter's history (the other counter keeps its own) and the ratio fills again from then on.
  • Forecast as used. Each published plan records its PV forecast for the current hour (scaled up from the remainder when the plan was solved mid-hour). The fullest plan of the hour is kept; a plan that covers less than half of the hour is not recorded. The current, unfinished hour is not compared.
  • Storage. One small row per hour: about 31 days of counter values and 15 days of forecasts, kept in the integration's own store (energy_compass.<entry_id>.calibration), saved at each new hour and on unload, restored on start. An invalid store is dropped with a warning.

Superseded results

If inputs change while a solve runs, the finished result is still published when only inputs (not configuration) changed — it is fresher than the retained plan — and a new solve follows. Configuration, registry and invalid-input changes discard in-flight results.

Alert and forecast validity

Forecast valid (binary_sensor.<name>_forecast_valid)

State Condition
on A published plan exists and now < valid_until. This holds during retries and while a retained plan still covers now.
off No plan, or its coverage/lifetime has ended. Recommendations become unavailable.

Attribute current_guidance_valid is true only when the consumption probe for the current interval produced a known level. Other attributes: coverage_end, requested_end, coverage_complete, input_ages, missing_sources, load_quality.

Alert (binary_sensor.<name>_alert)

code EN / PL Condition
invalid_input Invalid input / Nieprawidłowe dane wejściowe Any input validation failure (see optimizer status).
soc_measurement_jump SOC measurement jump / Skok wskazania SOC Between two reports SOC changed by more than battery power × elapsed time + soc_jump_percent (default 2 %) of capacity. Downward jumps alert immediately; upward jumps (BMS recalibration near full) first show calculating/soc_rebase_pending and alert only if not confirmed within 300 s. Recovery needs fresh plausible reports spanning ≥ 60 s.
timeout Calculation timeout / Przekroczony czas obliczeń Solve or worker deadline exceeded.
infeasible No feasible plan / Brak wykonalnego planu No plan satisfies the hard constraints.
error Calculation error / Błąd obliczeń Other failure.
inverter_clock_skew Inverter clock skew / Przesunięty zegar falownika Only with the Deye controller: the inverter clock differs from Home Assistant time by more than 5 minutes for 10 minutes (Inverter clock). Not a calculation failure: the plan is unaffected and plan_retained stays as it is.

Attributes: code, reason, since, plan_retained, last_successful_plan_at, clock_skew_minutes (empty unless the inverter clock alert is on). A retry does not clear the alert; only a successful new plan does. The inverter clock alert is the exception: it clears when the skew is back under 5 minutes. When a calculation failure and a clock skew coincide, code and reason show the calculation failure.

Plan retention

A retained plan is never extended beyond its original coverage and is not carried across an integration reload or Home Assistant restart. Saving Configure does not reload the integration, so it does not end the plan: see Saving options. The Deye controller keeps its own accepted copy of the plan across an entry reload, but drops it at a restart.

Operating modes — the planned battery state

The Energy compass sensor shows the operating mode of the current interval; every row of the plan's intervals attribute carries dispatch_mode. There are six modes. Per interval of h hours: activity = minimum_mode_power_kw × h (default 0.1 kW) and surplus = max(PV − load, 0).

Mode EN meaning Occurs when (physical flows) Allowed only if
CHARGE_GRID Charge from grid Battery charge ≥ surplus + activity — more is charged than PV surplus can supply, so the grid feeds the battery. No discharge, no curtailment. allow_grid_charge on; price ≤ grid-charge ceiling when that limit is on.
CHARGE_PV Charge from PV activity ≤ charge ≤ surplus — only solar surplus charges. No discharge, no curtailment. Load-following: grid export only while the charge is at its power limit or the battery is full. PV surplus exists.
DISCHARGE_GRID Discharge with export Discharge ≥ activity and grid export ≥ activity — the battery sells energy. allow_battery_export on; grid export capacity > 0; Sell only PV budget and export-benefit hurdle allow it.
SELF_CONSUME Self-consumption Discharge ≥ activity, no charge, no export, no curtailment — the battery covers the house. Load-following: grid import only while the discharge is at its power limit or the battery is emptied to its reserve. SOC above operating reserve.
HOLD Hold No charge, no discharge, no curtailment — the battery idles; the grid/PV cover load. Always available.
CURTAIL Curtail PV Curtailment ≥ activity, no discharge; the pack charges beside it only where the PV above what the site passes is more than the charge power takes (below). allow_curtailment on; without it, only the PV that the export cap or the inverter rating cannot pass that the pack cannot take, by its room or by its charge power (a forced spill, below).

When mode duration is disabled (minimum_mode_minutes = 0), the display state is derived from flows by precedence: CURTAIL → CHARGE_GRID → CHARGE_PV → DISCHARGE_GRID → SELF_CONSUME → HOLD.

A planned LFP balance hold does not add a mode: its rows reuse CHARGE_PV or CHARGE_GRID and carry balance_hold: true in the plan's intervals attribute.

Transitions and minimum duration

The diagram is simplified with HOLD as a hub: after its minimum duration any mode may be followed directly by any other available mode.

Rules (defaults: 60 min, 0.1 kW):

  • Every newly started mode — including HOLD and CURTAIL — lasts at least minimum_mode_minutes. Only a final passive HOLD/CURTAIL run may be clipped by coverage. The coordinator persists the accepted mode and its start; recalculation and restart preserve the clock.
  • SELF_CONSUME follows the load. The inverter discharges whatever the house draws, so the plan never pairs a small discharge with grid import: in a SELF_CONSUME interval the battery covers the whole demand, and import appears only once the discharge is at its interval power limit or the battery has been emptied to its reserve. Otherwise the row is HOLD with full import. The rule also holds with minimum_mode_minutes = 0: there are no modes then, and the discharge in any interval the flows label SELF_CONSUME is bound the same way. A carried CHARGE_PV/SELF_CONSUME commitment is executed the same way. If the battery runs out before it ends, the rest of the commitment is HOLD with full import (it starts no clock of its own: the commitment's deadline stays the only one). The same happens — from the first interval if need be — when the battery cannot cover the house and still keep the inverter standby loss (idle_drain_kw) of the later intervals, with no PV or grid charge to pay it in time. HOLD starts only in an interval without a PV surplus the pack could take, in every committed interval: with one, the row stays CHARGE_PV. A committed interval in which neither mode has anything to follow (net load and PV surplus both below minimum_mode_power_kw × h, for example a night base load under 100 W) is HOLD by classification and does not end the commitment: the plan bridges it (no HOLD clock starts, and the persisted commitment keeps its mode and start) or, when the battery is spent or full, starts a real HOLD run there as in any other interval (dispatch_policy.carried_idle_starts lists the bridged intervals). With a full battery on a site that cannot pass the PV, such an interval may be CURTAIL as well, like any other committed interval; it is then not bridged. When the terminal rule cannot be met afterwards (preserve_initial with no later PV or grid charge to refill what the house drew) the interval is a HOLD with full import, as for a spent battery, and the battery ends where it began. The plan is infeasible until the commitment ends when the daily throughput budget cannot pay the minimum activity the commitment asks for; the rare remaining cases (a standby loss or the preserve_initial terminal requirement that only PV surplus the plan cannot bank could cover) are listed in model and limitations. A direction the legacy direction guard blocks (initial_battery_mode) is not open: a pack that may not charge has no CHARGE_PV to follow and one that may not discharge has no SELF_CONSUME, so an interval with only that direction to follow is bridged too. A flexible-load probe is bridged the same way, as long as the probe it takes leaves the interval idle; a PV surplus it takes below the minimum activity is not one the pack could take, so HOLD may start on it.
  • CHARGE_PV follows the surplus. The inverter charges with every watt the house does not use, so the plan never pairs a partial charge with grid export: in a CHARGE_PV interval the battery takes the whole PV surplus, and export appears only once the charge is at its interval power limit or the battery has been filled to its upper bound. Otherwise the row is not CHARGE_PV. The rule also holds with minimum_mode_minutes = 0: there are no modes then, and the charge in any interval the flows label CHARGE_PV is bound the same way. A carried CHARGE_PV/SELF_CONSUME commitment is held to the same rule. If the battery is full before it ends (the next interval could not take even the minimum activity above the upper bound), the rest of the commitment is HOLD with the surplus exported, or CURTAIL where the site cannot pass the surplus (above the export cap or the inverter rating), as the inverter does with a full pack. The released HOLD starts no clock of its own — the commitment's deadline stays the only one — so it may turn to CURTAIL (which starts its own clock) before then. A released HOLD goes back to CHARGE_PV/SELF_CONSUME in any later interval of the commitment while the pack is still depleted: the pack takes the surplus, and a HOLD could not pass the PV above the export cap (on a site with grid_export_kw = 0 that is every sunrise). A HOLD released from a depleted pack also goes back in an interval whose PV the site cannot pass, where a HOLD has no legal flow: a plan followed one interval would otherwise reach the next boundary with a carried commitment and no plan. A HOLD released from a full pack does not go back there: it keeps its own clock across the boundary, and where the site cannot pass the PV it is CURTAIL (above). Nor does it go back because the terminal rule has spent the pack: that counts for the release and for the return of a HOLD that began on a depleted pack (the coordinator carries it as released), not for this one, which returns only when the pack is depleted in itself. A pack exactly at the reserve (the inverter's usual empty state) is depleted in this sense, not a safety exception: a carried SELF_CONSUME there is released and charges like one 0.01 kWh above the reserve. Where that released HOLD has no plan (a commitment no plan can keep) the house is still never left without one. The plan is the first of these that has a solution, each tried only when the one before has none and all within the recalculation's one time budget: the release; the commitment's own HOLD with its clock, as the safety exception below, which curtails where curtailment is allowed; the plan without the commitment (only for a carried CHARGE_PV or SELF_CONSUME, which a plan followed one interval can leave in a state its own minimum duration then makes infeasible). After that last plan a first mode that is still CHARGE_PV or SELF_CONSUME keeps the commitment and its clock; any other first mode starts a clock of its own. The return is the commitment going on, not a new run: the commitment's deadline stays the only clock. A pack that empties again inside the same commitment is released again and goes back again, as often as the commitment lasts. The release survives the interval boundary: the plan marks the rows of such a HOLD (dispatch_policy.released_hold_starts) and the coordinator keeps the commitment and its start, flagged as released, instead of recording a HOLD with a clock of its own, so the next plan goes back to CHARGE_PV as the first one published. That HOLD may go on past the commitment's deadline without a clock; a return to CHARGE_PV/SELF_CONSUME after the deadline is a run of its own and gets a fresh start. The first committed interval is judged the same way against the observed state of charge: a pack already within the lowered ceiling of that interval (for example after the interval that filled it was carried out) may be HOLD or CURTAIL at once, in either member mode. An observed state of charge at the upper bound is the safety exception below. A committed interval in which the pack fills while the rest of the surplus is still above the export cap or the inverter rating is planned: CHARGE_PV cannot fill the pack and curtail in the same interval, so the pack counts as full for the next interval, which may be HOLD or CURTAIL, once it is within that interval's curtail need of the ceiling (the PV that must go to the pack or be curtailed, at least the minimum activity). With minimum_mode_minutes = 0 the rule costs solve time (see the table in model and limitations). A site that cannot curtail (allow_curtailment off) with grid export capped, or the inverter rated below the PV, would be left with PV that has nowhere to go once the pack is full. In most cases it is planned rather than reported as infeasible (measured below): the PV above what the cap and the inverter can pass (the curtail need; with a minimum duration at least the minimum activity) is spilled in an interval whose pack cannot take it, labelled CURTAIL (the inverter throttles by itself; the Deye controller runs the PV charge profile at the planned current on a row that charges and its HOLD profile on one that charges nothing). The gate is the room of the pack: the interval starts at or above the ceiling less what the pack would have to absorb, so a pack with a little room that cannot take the surplus spills too, and a pack that can take it never does, whatever the sell price. The part the pack cannot take by its charge power (the curtail need less charge_kw × h) is spilled whatever the room: the pack charges at its power and the inverter throttles the rest in the same interval, so a pack with room and a charge power below the surplus has a plan. With a minimum duration a CURTAIL run keeps the next interval's gate open (it discharges nothing, so the pack only drifts down by its standby loss, or rises where the row charges), a CHARGE_PV or SELF_CONSUME run may end in CURTAIL when the pack fills inside it (or in HOLD when the PV it had to take is over as well), and room left below the gate stays empty during a CURTAIL interval until the next replanning reads the real state of charge. A CURTAIL run carried into the next plan keeps spilling while the need lasts, also when the pack has dropped below full meanwhile. A site that can pass its PV is unchanged. Measured on seeded sweeps (2400 problems solved once): with the spill 533 of 589 are planned at minimum duration 0, 565 of 606 at 15 minutes, 582 of 620 at 30 minutes and 503 of 585 at 60 minutes (without it 171, 160, 149 and 97). A bell-shaped day followed interval by interval to its end keeps a plan all the way in 207 of 214 days at 15 minutes, 172 of 189 at 30 minutes and 158 of 197 at 60 minutes (without the spill 27, 23 and 23); most of the others have no plan from the first interval.
