The rest stay without a plan, as before, mainly for two reasons the plan does not cover: a HOLD run that the plan itself starts and that meets PV the site cannot pass while the pack has room (the spill there would be the plan's own choice), more often at 60 minutes, and some draws with a flexible-load probe. The forced part (T-066) cut the 2400 problems solved once without a plan from 226 to 76, and the rolling draws not followed from 190 to 57 of 1800, with no problem solved once that main planned newly infeasible; of 3600 days followed interval by interval on four seeds one that main follows to its end stops at a boundary with no plan on any site. A carried HOLD or CURTAIL commitment more often leaves a plan (T-082): where the site cannot pass the PV, a CURTAIL takes the carried HOLD over with room in the pack, in the intervals of that run where nothing is forced, and a CURTAIL run goes on through an interval with no need, while it is inside its minimum duration, into a need that comes back smaller than the room; that cut the 2400 draws without a plan from 76 to 38 and the rolling draws not followed from 57 to 16 of 1800, with none newly infeasible (counts, better and worse draws and commits in the model document) (model and limitations).
  • CURTAIL goes on through a PV gap. A CURTAIL run lasts the minimum duration, and PV can drop inside it. A HOLD in an interval with PV below the minimum activity (minimum_mode_power_kw × h) inside that duration is the run going on, not a new HOLD: the inverter has nothing to curtail and the pack and the grid do what HOLD does. It counts for the CURTAIL clock, starts no HOLD clock, and ends with the run's duration; the HOLD after it starts its own clock. It applies to a run begun by PV that the export cap or the inverter cannot pass, and to a CURTAIL carried in; dispatch_policy.carried_idle_starts lists these rows too, and the persisted commitment keeps its mode and start there. It holds inside a carried CHARGE_PV/SELF_CONSUME commitment as well (a CURTAIL released from it goes on through a PV gap within the commitment's own duration), and for an interval with a load below the minimum activity.
  • CURTAIL takes over a HOLD that cannot pass the PV. HOLD takes no curtailment, so a HOLD that has to last (a carried HOLD, the HOLD that the safety exception below puts in place of a CHARGE_PV at the maximum state of charge, or a HOLD that began earlier in the plan, for example after a CURTAIL run that ended in a PV gap) has no legal mode in an interval whose PV, after the house, is above the export cap (grid_export_kw) or above the inverter rating. There the inverter curtails by itself and the interval is CURTAIL: it takes the HOLD over and from then on is an ordinary CURTAIL run with its own minimum duration (which outlasts the HOLD's remainder; a PV gap inside it is bridged as above). Only where the site cannot pass the PV: anywhere else CURTAIL inside a HOLD's duration would be a label to leave it with, and is not offered. The HOLD after the run starts its own clock. A HOLD released from a carried CHARGE_PV/SELF_CONSUME commitment has no clock of its own and is not taken over. A flexible-load probe counts: its load is part of what the site passes, so the takeover is offered only for the probe loads that leave PV above the cap.
  • CURTAIL charges what the pack can take. When the PV above what the site passes (above the export cap after the house, or above the inverter rating) is more than the pack takes by its charge power in one interval, neither CHARGE_PV (which curtails nothing) nor a CURTAIL that charged nothing could hold it; the inverter charges at the charge power and curtails the rest, and so does the plan: the interval is CURTAIL, with the charge between zero and the PV left after the house. What the pack takes there is PV only: a CURTAIL interval that charges imports nothing, not even for the house. Where the pack is at the reserve under a carried CHARGE_PV/SELF_CONSUME commitment (a sunrise on a zero-export site with a 1 kW pack and 3.6 kW of PV) this is the plan itself, not a fallback. In a carried commitment CURTAIL is offered in such an interval whatever the pack held before; with a flexible-load probe, only for the probe loads that leave PV beyond the pack. The CURTAIL that opens such a run goes on through the run's minimum duration: the later intervals of the commitment offer CURTAIL while it is under way, also where the PV is no longer beyond the pack (it does not charge there, so a pack at the reserve waits for the end of the run: up to 105 minutes after the first interval at a minimum duration of 120), because the run may not change mode inside its duration and the commitment's CHARGE_PV is not a way out of it. With allow_curtailment off such an interval is planned only as a forced spill, where the pack has less room than the PV the site cannot pass: the CURTAIL interval then charges what the pack takes and spills the rest. The same holds for a pack with room: it charges at its power and spills the PV beyond it, whatever its room.
  • PV-follow group: CHARGE_PV and SELF_CONSUME share one clock — in both the inverter charges from surplus and covers a deficit from the battery, so flipping between them is not a mode change.
  • Any other change (source, destination, HOLD or CURTAIL) starts a new clock, except the HOLD released from a full pack or an empty battery above, which has none. Idle HOLD cannot fund an active run.
  • Coverage: a new active mode needs a full duration of forecast coverage remaining.
  • Safety exception (pause, not reset): during an unexpired active commitment the current row shows HOLD when the observed SOC is already at the upper bound (charging modes — observed_soc_maximum) or at/below the reserve (discharge modes — observed_soc_minimum; not a carried SELF_CONSUME, which is released as a depleted pack above, unless that release has no plan), or when a carried CHARGE_GRID meets a price above the ceiling before its deadline (grid_charge_price_limit). The interrupted mode and deadline stay stored; no other mode may start before that deadline, except the CURTAIL that takes the HOLD over where the site cannot pass the PV (above). Exposed in dispatch_policy.safety_exception.
  • Strategy change (reset): writing a new strategy drops the carried commitment for the next plan, which starts unlocked (see strategy-switch release).
  • Setting minimum_mode_minutes = 0 disables duration and minimum-power rules; the SELF_CONSUME and CHARGE_PV load-following rules stay on.

Policies that gate modes

Policy Default Effect
Sell only PV (limit_export_to_pv) on Per local day: exported energy ≤ PV generated (observed since midnight + forecast). Requires pv_energy_today and grid_export_energy_today counters.
Export limit scope (export_limit_scope) local_day local_day checks the budget once for the whole day; produced checks it as a running total so export can never run ahead of PV generated so far that day. See Sell only PV.
Limit grid-charging price (limit_grid_charge_price, maximum_grid_charge_price) off CHARGE_GRID only at buy price ≤ ceiling for its whole minimum duration.
Minimum export benefit (minimum_export_episode_benefit) 1 currency unit Each additional battery-export period must improve full-horizon cost by at least this amount. 0 disables.
Minimum grid-charge episode benefit (minimum_grid_charge_episode_benefit) 0 (off) Same hurdle for new grid-charge periods; consolidates charging into fewer episodes.
Import penalty (import_penalty_per_kwh) 0 Planning-only shadow price per imported kWh, under every strategy.
HOLD forecast-miss charge (built in, not a setting) 0.5 of the forecast load Planning-only charge on HOLD and CURTAIL in an interval with PV above its load, where the buy price exceeds what a stored kWh can still earn or save later: the plan stores the surplus (CHARGE_PV) instead of holding the pack through a peak for a few watts of export. Not a ban: a HOLD worth more is still planned. Never in a published cost. See HOLD and CURTAIL at a peak price.
Deposit model (deposit_model) off off is the setting for every site. manual (experimental) values exported energy and the deposit-payable part of imports by a factor you state; measured on a one-year replay it did not lower the bill. Needs the distribution part of the buy price. See Net-billing deposit value.
Inverter standby loss (idle_drain_kw) 0 (off) Constant battery drain modelled per interval.
Battery buffer for expensive periods (peak_reserve_margin_kwh) 0 (off) Energy kept above the forecast need when an expensive period starts. See Peak-period reserve.
Battery buffer after battery export (export_reserve_margin_kwh) 0 (off) Energy kept above the forecast need after each battery export inside an expensive period, until the next cheap interval. Its own setting (does not follow the buffer above); needs battery export and Limit grid-charging price. See Peak-period reserve.
Terminal rule (terminal_mode) preserve_initial End SOC ≥ start SOC, or value: stored energy at the end is credited at terminal_value_per_kwh.

Setup profiles can pre-fill the import penalty, standby loss and terminal rule for new installations; see Setup profiles.

Net-billing deposit value

Under Polish net billing the value of exported energy is booked on the prosumer deposit, and the deposit pays only what you owe the seller for energy; distribution charges are paid in cash. After 12 months the unused part is refunded, but a month's refund cannot exceed ρ × the value exported in that month (ρ = 30 % with hourly RCE settlement, 20 % with monthly RCEm), where the value is the export value without the 1.23 coefficient; the rest is void. While the deposit is short, or its unused part still fits under the cap, one currency unit of export or of energy-part import is worth exactly one unit of cash and the planner needs no correction. Once the cap binds, one more unit of export is worth only ρ/1.23 of a sell price that contains the 1.23 coefficient (0.244 for ρ = 30 %, 0.163 for 20 %) and the energy part of an import costs nothing in cash (it is paid from money that would expire). The deposit model lets the planner see that, but it does not pay off: off is the setting for every site, also a site whose deposit is forfeited, and manual is experimental. The auto model was withdrawn; a stored auto is read as off without an error or an Alert. off is the default and then the plan is byte-identical to a build without the model.

What was measured, on a one-year replay of 40 hourly-RCE homes with a 10 kWh battery, billed by the yearly formula and by the monthly ledger:

  • no factor lowered the yearly bill by more than 44 PLN, and the factor at the cap raised it in all 40 homes, by 68–431 PLN (yearly formula) or 21–306 PLN (monthly ledger);
  • with monthly RCEm the factor changes the bill by less than 10 PLN;
  • a site whose deposit is forfeited sets nothing: deposit_model stays off. Switching battery export off because of a forfeited deposit cost 154–662 PLN a year in all 16 homes measured (with grid charging and battery export allowed).

Two parts of the buy price. The model must know which part of a buy price is energy (payable by the deposit) and which is distribution (paid in cash). The buy price of an interval is the sum of the two, and you give the distribution part as rates, never the energy part:

included:  buy = buy source price                  (the source is an all-in price, e.g. a tariff schedule)
added:     buy = buy source price + distribution   (the source is the energy price only)
energy part = clamp(buy − distribution, 0, max(buy, 0))

Use added for a dynamic energy price (a forecast such as RCE-based tariffs) or a price list typed as on the invoice. It changes the buy price itself, for the planner and for reported costs, and works with the deposit model off. Example: dynamic energy price 0.25 at midday and 0.95 in the evening peak plus the G12 distribution rate 0.540 give buy prices 0.79 and 1.49; at night 0.45 + 0.143 give 0.593. When the cap binds the planner sees only the distribution part: 0.540, 0.540 and 0.143. A negative energy price keeps its real price and has no energy part to waive.

Setting (Tariffs) Default Meaning
deposit_model off off: full prices, the setting for every site. manual (experimental): you state export_value_factor. A stored auto (withdrawn) is read as off.
deposit_refund_percent 30 ρ, the refund cap as a share of a month's export value. 20 for monthly RCEm settlement. A seller that refunds a share of the deposit (which contains the 1.23 coefficient) has 36.9 / 24.6 here.
export_value_factor 1.0 manual only: what one more unit of export is worth (0–1).
buy_distribution_mode included included or added, as above.
buy_distribution_rate, buy_distribution_mid_peak_rate, buy_distribution_off_peak_rate 0 Everything the distributor bills per kWh (network rate, quality, RES and cogeneration fees), typed like the buy rate or pre-filled; the first is the peak or single zone, the second the mid-peak zone (G13 only), the third the off-peak zone. VAT applies when buy_apply_vat is on; buy_multiplier, buy_addition and a forecast floor apply to the buy source only. The zones come from the tariff schedule of the buy source or from a distribution tariff; with neither, or with G11, the first rate applies all day. With two zones set both rates or neither, with three zones all three or none: a partly set group fails the calculation closed. The monthly fee belongs in monthly_charge.

The cap pressure π (0 = deposit short or within the cap, 1 = cap binding) gives two factors that exist only inside the optimizer:

export value factor  φx = 1 − π × (1 − ρp)    1 → ρp,  ρp = ρ / 1.23
import energy factor φe = 1 − π               1 → 0
planning buy  = buy − (1 − φe) × energy part of buy
planning sell = φx × max(sell, 0) + min(sell, 0)
  • manual (experimental): φx is your export_value_factor as typed, even below ρp. Only π is derived from it, π = clamp((1 − φx) / (1 − ρp), 0, 1), so φe = 1 − π follows (a value at or below ρp devalues the energy part of imports fully). At the cap (π = 1) φx is ρp = ρ / 1.23, not ρ: 0.244 for 30 %, 0.163 for 20 %. With deposit_refund_percent 100 it is 1/1.23, not 1; the setting that never cancels anything is deposit_model: off.
  • No distribution part (the distribution rates are 0): the whole buy price would count as deposit-payable and an import would look free. With π above 0 φe is therefore forced to 1 and reason is split_missing; φx still applies. Set the distribution rates to use the model.
  • Negative sell prices stay whole: the factor scales only the positive part, because a negative price is a real charge.
  • Reported costs do not change. Net cost, Plan.grid_cost, the cost sensors, consumption levels and the maximum_grid_charge_price ceiling all stay at invoice prices; only the planning objective uses the factors, under every strategy and before the strategy weights.
  • Battery sale threshold, worked example (PGE G12 2026 gross prices, round trip 0.89, wear 0.05 per kWh): selling from the battery and buying the energy back at night pays above about 0.73 currency/kWh while the cap is not binding. With the cap binding the threshold is about 0.88 at ρ = 30 % and about 1.31 at ρ = 20 % (a seller that refunds 36.9 % / 24.6 % of the deposit: about 0.71 / 1.07). What changes with the cap binding is the use of surplus PV (worth 0.40 × ρp = 0.10 instead of 0.40 at a sell price of 0.40 and ρ = 30 %, so it goes to the battery and flexible load first) and night grid charging, which stays profitable.

Diagnostics are in the plan attribute dispatch_policy.settlement:

Key Meaning
model off or manual
export_value_factor, import_energy_factor φx and φe the optimizer used
cap_pressure π
refund_percent the input used (ρ in percent)
distribution_mode included or added
reason ok, off or split_missing (π above 0 but no distribution part, φe forced to 1)

Peak-period reserve

The load forecast is a mean, so a plan that drains the battery exactly to the reserve by the end of an expensive period falls short on roughly every second day. peak_reserve_margin_kwh asks the solver to enter each expensive period with that much energy on top of the forecast need. It requires Limit grid-charging price: an expensive period is a run of intervals whose buy price is above maximum_grid_charge_price, i.e. where the battery cannot be refilled from the grid. The target applies to the end of the cheap interval right before the run:

entry target = min(usable capacity, reserve + peak_reserve_margin_kwh + run deficit / η_discharge)

where the deficit sums max(0, load − PV) over the run. Intervals inside the run carry no target: the plan is recalculated during the run, and a target there would make it buy at the expensive price to rebuild the buffer once the house had used it — the opposite of what the buffer is for. For the same reason a run that is already in progress when the plan is calculated gets no target, nor does a run where PV covers the house. The target is soft: a shortfall is billed at the median expensive price minus the ceiling and reported as peak_reserve_shortfall_kwh; reported costs never include it. Inside the run the buffer is ordinary stored energy, so the plan may still export it when selling pays more than the later purchase — down to the forecast need, plus export_reserve_margin_kwh when that is set, not below (next paragraph). It works in every strategy, next to the autonomy floor. Warnings: peak_reserve_requires_grid_charge_ceiling (setting above 0 while the ceiling is off) and peak_reserve_inactive (no upcoming expensive run with a deficit in the horizon).

Buffer under an export. export_reserve_margin_kwh (default 0 = off) is its own setting: it does not follow peak_reserve_margin_kwh, and a site that already runs the entry buffer keeps its plans and solve times until this one is set. It needs battery export and Limit grid-charging price (warnings export_reserve_requires_battery_export and export_reserve_requires_grid_charge_ceiling). It applies inside the run, but only to an interval in which the plan exports from the battery: there the battery must keep reserve + export_reserve_margin_kwh + deficit until the next cheap interval / η_discharge after the interval. An interval without an export has no target, so a recalculation during the run never buys at the expensive price to rebuild the buffer; the plan simply stops exporting. The target is soft, billed at the median buy price of those intervals (what a missing kWh of buffer costs when the load runs above the forecast) and counted in peak_reserve_shortfall_kwh. The plan therefore keeps the buffer as long as the export earns less than that purchase would cost: the cheapest export interval shrinks first. Only intervals where sell price × η_discharge is above the grid-charging ceiling carry a target, and a run that no cheap interval follows in the horizon has none. Cost: it adds rows, and the solve is slower where the buffer binds. In the benchmark sweep (40 days of 96 and 192 intervals, binding days only) 0.5 kWh gave up 0.7 of 3.6 kWh of battery export on the evening-window days, left the slowest solve at 2.4 to 3.9 s at 96 intervals (5.0 to 6.1 s at 192) and ended none at the 10 s limit; from 0.75 kWh the solve of a long evening run took 4 to 6 times longer at its median and some days reached the limit (1 of 40 at 96 intervals and 0.75 kWh, 4 of 40 at 192 intervals and 1.0 kWh). Raise the setting in steps and check time_limited on the plan (details in model.md); at 0 nothing changes.

Sizing of the entry buffer: 0.25–0.75 kWh is a reasonable start. In a backtest on one household with a two-zone tariff, 0.5 kWh halved the mornings that ran out before PV (42 % → 21 %) at roughly neutral cost: the buffer is not lost, it is used later or valued at the end of the horizon.

Consumption levels — BOOST, CHEAP, NORMAL, LIMIT

The Consumption compass answers "how attractive is using one more kWh in this interval?". For each display interval (default 60 min over 24 h) the solver reruns with probe_kwh (default 1 kWh) of extra load. Consumption cost = (probe plan cost − base plan cost) ÷ added kWh. Because the battery and grid are re-optimized, this is the true marginal cost — it can differ from the tariff price (e.g. solar that would otherwise be exported costs its lost export value).

Level EN / PL Condition Typical situation
BOOST Boost / Zwiększone zużycie Cost strictly below boost_ceiling (default 0.01 currency/kWh). Free or negative energy: surplus PV that cannot be stored or exported, negative prices. Run everything you can.
CHEAP Cheap / Tanio Not BOOST, and cost ≤ cheap_percentile (default 25th) of reference costs, or ≤ the minimum purchase tariff in the reference horizon. Among the cheapest hours of the reference window. Good time for flexible loads.
LIMIT Limit / Ograniczenie Cost strictly above both limit_floor (default 1 currency/kWh) and the limit_percentile (default 75th). Expensive peak — extra use forces costly import or loses valuable export. Postpone.
NORMAL Normal / Normalnie Anything else. Average conditions.
unknown — The probe failed or ran out of time, or the interval lies beyond forecast coverage. Entity unavailable; later windows can still be known.

Percentiles come from successful probe costs across the reference horizon (default 24 h) using linear interpolation. If a full reference probe fails, short_coverage decides: absolute_fallback (default: keep BOOST/LIMIT absolute rules and the minimum-tariff CHEAP rule) or unavailable.

Limit: probes that do not finish in time. Every probe is a full, exact solve of the whole planning horizon and is known only when it finishes within probe_time_limit_s (default 2 s); the probes run one after another inside total_time_limit_s (default 60 s). A probe that does not finish stays unknown — it is never replaced by an approximate cost. One unknown full reference probe is enough for short_coverage (reason is reference_probe_failed), and an interval whose own probe is unknown has no level.

How long a probe takes depends on the strategy and on the number of intervals in the planning horizon. self_sufficiency and backup_ready keep SELF_CONSUME on through the night, and the load-following rule makes their probes many times slower. Probes with a known cost at the default limits, quarter-hour prices and hourly display intervals, measured on a fast desktop CPU (Apple M4 Max):

Planning horizon cost_min, pv_swap, max_export, grid_friendly self_sufficiency backup_ready
12 h (48 intervals), 12 probes 12 of 12 12 of 12 12 of 12
24 h (96 intervals, the default), 24 probes 24 of 24 0 of 24 2 of 24
48 h (192 intervals), 24 probes 7–23 of 24 none none

So with self_sufficiency or backup_ready the consumption levels are unknown for nearly every interval already on the default 24 h horizon, and on a 48 h horizon no strategy completes its probes (with a 15-minute display interval 18–67 of 96 are known). At 48 h the base plan of these two strategies also runs into solve_time_limit_s and is published as time_limited. minimum_mode_minutes = 0 does not lift the limit: at 24 h 1 of 24 (self_sufficiency) and 8 to 17 of 24 (backup_ready) probes are known, which is still short_coverage. A slower host, such as a Raspberry Pi, reaches each limit at a shorter horizon.

The flexible energy depth is bound by the same two settings: each of its five solves gets probe_time_limit_s, inside what the probes left of total_time_limit_s. With self_sufficiency or backup_ready at 24 h none of the five finished within the default 2 s, so the depth is unknown (profiles UNKNOWN, reason timeout); cost_min at 24 h and self_sufficiency at 12 h got all five.

What was measured to help on the same host, at the default 24 h horizon:

  • backup_ready: probe_time_limit_s 10 and total_time_limit_s 120 gave all 24 probes (47 s of probing per recalculation) and, with the same probe limit, all five flexible-depth solves (21 s more). With probe_time_limit_s 5 one probe was still late and the levels stayed on short_coverage.
  • self_sufficiency: only the maximum of both settings, probe_time_limit_s 30 and total_time_limit_s 300, gave all 24 probes, after 199 s of probing per recalculation, and the five flexible-depth solves took 48 s more. That leaves no headroom for a slower host or a harder day.
  • A 12 h planning horizon gave all 12 probes for both strategies at the default limits, with the slowest self_sufficiency probe at 1.5 s of the 2 s limit; the plan then looks 12 h ahead only.

The table, the per-probe times and the command that reproduces them are in docs/runtime-validation.md.

Windows and flexible energy depth

Windows

Adjacent intervals of the same level merge into windows. next_boost_start, next_cheap_start and next_limit_start show the start of the active or next window of that kind; next_change shows the next known different level.

Attribute status Condition
active Window start ≤ now < end.
upcoming Window starts later within coverage.
none_in_coverage No such window in the forecast; the entity is unavailable.

start_basis is forecast, or first_observed when an already active window keeps its first observed start across recalculations and restarts. next_change stops at unknown coverage rather than guessing.

Flexible energy depth

Answers "how much deferrable energy can I use cheaply?". The solver independently places 3, 5, 10, 15 and 20 kWh blocks at up to flexible_load_max_power_kw (default 3 kW).

Profile status Condition
ANCHOR The 3 kWh profile; its average incremental cost is the anchor price.
STABLE Marginal block cost ≤ anchor + flexible_price_degradation_percent (default 15 %) of
DEGRADED Marginal block cost above that threshold — stops the published depth.
UNKNOWN Not solved: insufficient_time (block cannot fit at max power within the horizon), timeout, or a solver reason. Stops the depth.

Groups: small (3/5 kWh), medium (10/15 kWh), large (20 kWh).

A block that has no solution on the problem the plan was solved for is tried again on the later rungs of the plan's own ladder (the commitment's HOLD, then the plan without the commitment), each against the plan of that rung, so a level is never priced against a plan of another problem. It is only a carried CHARGE_PV/SELF_CONSUME commitment whose plan sits on the edge of a full pack that needs this. Two neighbouring levels solved on different rungs have no block cost between them, and a level on another rung than the first (anchor) level is not judged against the anchor's allowed price: both are UNKNOWN. A level is published with the reason that ended it: infeasible only if every rung it reached had no solution, while a timeout or another solver error ends it at once as that error.

Dispatch strategies

select.<name>_strategy chooses which objective bundle the solver uses. Every strategy keeps all hard physical constraints; strategies change only planning weights and a small set of policy flags. Reported costs (expected_net_cost, consumption cost) always stay real currency — strategy penalties never appear in them.

Strategy EN / PL label Goal Typical use
cost_min Cost minimisation / Minimalizacja kosztów Lowest total cost Default, everyday
self_sufficiency Self-sufficiency / Samowystarczalność Fewest grid kWh Flat prices, off-grid preference, zero/negative prices
backup_ready Backup ready / Gotowość awaryjna Keep a high reserve Storm warning, planned outage, winter
pv_swap PV swap / Zamiana energii PV Buy cheap at night, sell own PV later Small winter PV with an evening sell premium
max_export Maximum export / Maksymalny eksport Unrestricted arbitrage High sell-price windows
grid_friendly Grid friendly / Przyjazna dla sieci Flatten import/export peaks Capacity tariffs, weak connection

What each strategy changes

The solver minimizes

grid     = Σ ( import_weight × buy × import + import_kwh_weight × import
               − export_weight × (sell − pv_export_margin) × export )
           + battery_export_penalty_per_kwh × battery_export
autonomy = soc_target_weight × Σ (deepest shortfall per window below the autonomy floor)
peak     = peak_import_weight × max(import power)
caps     = cap_violation_weight × Σ (import/export above soft caps)
objective = grid + wear + episode hurdles + autonomy + peak + caps − terminal credit
Strategy Autonomy floor Sell only PV Grid-charge ceiling Export-benefit hurdle Weights
cost_min off user setting user setting user setting defaults (only import_penalty_per_kwh)
self_sufficiency on user setting user setting user setting import_kwh_weight = max(5.0, max |buy| + 0.50, import penalty); battery-export penalty 0.20/kWh
backup_ready on, floor ≥ 80 % capacity user setting user setting user setting floor weight ≥ 2.0/kWh
pv_swap on forced on forced off user setting sell price reduced by margin 0.05/kWh
max_export off forced off forced off forced 0 defaults
grid_friendly off user setting user setting user setting peak import 0.50/kW, soft-cap violation 2.0/kWh

"User setting" means the strategy leaves the option as configured. Forced values apply only to options the user has not set explicitly: any strategy-owned option that deviates from its shipped default is recorded in explicit_strategy_fields and is never overridden by a bundle.

All numbers above are defaults of Planning options: self_sufficiency_import_price_per_kwh (5.0), self_sufficiency_export_penalty_per_kwh (0.20), backup_target_soc_percent (80), backup_shortfall_price_per_kwh (2.0), pv_swap_margin_per_kwh (0.05), peak_import_price_per_kw (0.50), cap_violation_price_per_kwh (2.0), grid_friendly_import_cap_kw / _export_cap_kw (0 = site connection limit), autonomy_margin_per_kwh (0.10).

Autonomy floor (used by self_sufficiency, backup_ready, pv_swap)

The floor asks: will the battery carry the house through the next period where load exceeds PV? The horizon is split into windows by cumulative net surplus; within each window the target is

soc_target[t] = min(usable capacity, reserve + (1 / η_discharge) × Σ deficit until window end)

The deepest shortfall below the target is billed once per window at soc_target_weight = expected night rebuy price (median night buy price) + autonomy_margin_per_kwh. The floor looks 48 h ahead on PV/load forecasts even before tomorrow's prices are published. It is soft: violations become autonomy_shortfall_kwh on the plan instead of an infeasible solve. It needs a PV source (autonomy_floor_requires_pv otherwise).

LFP balance charge

LFP packs need a periodic full charge and a short hold at the top so the BMS can balance cells and re-anchor its SOC. With Periodic LFP balance charge (lfp_balance) on, Energy Compass tracks the last completed balance and plans the next one. The tracker itself keeps observing SOC and advancing its state even while lfp_balance is off; turning the setting on only starts publishing balance windows and the diagnostic sensor.

Setting Default Meaning
balance_interval_days 7 Days between completed balances
balance_hold_minutes 60 Minutes SOC must stay at or above the threshold
balance_soc_threshold 99 % SOC that counts as full
balance_value 5.0 Value of balancing on the due day

A balance completes after SOC stays at or above the threshold for the whole hold. A reading below the threshold restarts the hold. Only observed time counts: an unavailable or stale SOC gives no credit, and two full readings more than soc_max_age_seconds apart restart the hold from the later one (a hold whose last full reading is older than that is neither holding nor complete). Completion is evaluated lazily — while full readings keep arriving, the hold completes on the next check without needing a state change. Phases: ok → eligible (the earlier of 2 days or half the interval before due) → due; holding overlays whichever phase is active while a hold is running. A hold that starts while the balance is still ok (for example SOC back at 100 % the day after a balance) is tracked and completes, but is not scheduled: the optimizer gets no hold window and no miss cost for it.

The optimizer may pick one hour-aligned hold window: candidate windows start only on the whole hour, and while due, only within the next 24 h (an eligible balance may look anywhere across the horizon). Inside the chosen window SOC stays at or above the threshold and the battery does not discharge. Skipping costs 10 % of balance_value while eligible — small, so the planner normally balances only on cheap or free energy, but it still picks a grid window that costs less than that — balance_value × (1 + days overdue) once due, and 10 × balance_value during a hold that is eligible or due. A window is published as CHARGE_PV only when PV covers load in every one of its slots; otherwise (mixed PV/grid or pure grid, such as a night window) it is CHARGE_GRID, which additionally requires grid charging to be allowed and the grid-charge price ceiling (if any) to pass in every slot — with balance_hold: true on every row. With an optional pessimistic PV source the PV test is stricter. From the slot before the earliest candidate window to the horizon end, the battery's energy may rise up to full capacity instead of the configured SOC ceiling, so a hold is never blocked by soc_ceiling below 100 %; that lift only matters when the ceiling is below 100 %. Consumption probes keep the chosen window fixed so a probe's extra load prices the load, not the balance choice.

The Battery balance diagnostic sensor (sensor.<name>_battery_balance) reports ok, eligible, scheduled, holding or overdue, with last_completed, next_due, days_overdue, planned_start, planned_end, planned_mode, pv_series, hold_progress_minutes, hold_required_minutes, threshold_percent.

Pessimistic PV for the balance window

The balance window is chosen on the median PV forecast, so a low-PV day can leave the pack short of the threshold and the balance missed again. Sources → Add source → PV pessimistic (optional) binds a second, lower forecast of the same site (for Solcast, pv_estimate10; the Solcast presets propose that field). It takes the same interval-forecast mapping as a PV source; Review and edit sources lists, edits, extends with a continuation and removes it. It needs PV enabled. It can accompany either kind of PV source; the Energy dashboard solar forecast has no pessimistic series, so bind this one separately.

With it configured, a CHARGE_PV window is offered only if both hold on the pessimistic series:

  1. Pack: charging from PV surplus alone (pv − load, at eta_charge and charge_kw, no discharge) lifts the pack to the balance threshold by the window start.
  2. Window: PV covers load in every slot of the window.

Otherwise the start is offered only as CHARGE_GRID, subject to the usual grid-charge and price-ceiling rules, so the solver can pick a cheap grid window instead. The dispatch plan itself keeps using the median series. Without the source nothing changes.

The solver prices every window on the median series, where PV surplus can pay for a vetoed CHARGE_GRID window, so several starts would cost the same. To avoid a tie-break landing on an expensive slot, every CHARGE_GRID window offered while the pessimistic series is present (also one that is CHARGE_GRID on the median series alone) carries a ranking cost: the energy the pessimistic series leaves to the grid, that is what the pack still lacks to reach the threshold at the window start plus the load PV does not cover inside the window, at the window's buy prices. The solver adds 5 % of each window's excess over the cheapest window the solver can pick to that window's cost, so a window the pessimistic series still supports (CHARGE_PV) beats a vetoed one and, among vetoed ones, the cheapest wins. The addition never exceeds half the cost of skipping the balance. A start-0 window the pack cannot reach (it starts below the threshold) is left out of that comparison, so it never shifts the other windows towards a skip; the ranking can still tip a close call against the balance. It is a preference, not a strict tie-break: a start that is cheaper on the median series by more than 5 % of the difference in ranking cost still wins. It is not part of the plan's cost.

Trade-off: the pack test counts PV surplus only. A start the pack would reach only by charging from the grid before the window is offered as CHARGE_GRID alone, and is dropped when the grid-charge price ceiling blocks a slot of the window, so balance_no_window_in_horizon can appear where a window existed without the source.

The pv_series attribute of the Battery balance sensor and the balance_pv_series attribute of the plan sensor say which series decided the candidate windows: pessimistic when the source is configured and usable, median otherwise (also without the source); null when lfp_balance is off or there is no battery. The source is optional input and never invalidates the plan. If it is unavailable, stale, malformed, negative or does not cover the horizon, the windows fall back to the median series and the plan carries the balance_pessimistic_pv_unavailable warning. A source going stale raises no state change, so the fallback takes effect at the next periodic recalculation (refresh_minutes) or source change.

cost_min — cost minimisation

  • Goal: lowest forecast cost: purchases − sales + battery wear − terminal credit.
  • Changes: nothing; byte-identical to the plain model when import_penalty_per_kwh = 0.
  • Behaviour: charges when energy is cheap (grid or PV), discharges into expensive hours, exports only when the spread beats losses, wear and the export-benefit hurdle.
  • Choose when: everyday operation; the default and the fallback of the switch blueprint.
  • Watch out: it may leave the battery low before a cheap-looking night if forecasts are wrong — no autonomy reserve.

self_sufficiency — self-sufficiency

  • Goal: minimize grid kWh, not currency.
  • Changes: every imported kWh costs at least max(5.0, highest |buy price| + 0.50, import_penalty_per_kwh), so import always dominates price differences; battery export costs an extra 0.20/kWh; autonomy floor on.
  • Behaviour: fills the battery from PV, avoids grid charging and battery export unless needed, keeps enough energy for the next deficit window.
  • Choose when: day/night price spread is small (the blueprint picks it when the spread is below 0.15 PLN/kWh), when prices are zero or negative, or when independence matters more than cost.
  • Watch out: reported costs stay real — this strategy can cost more money than cost_min.

backup_ready — backup ready

  • Goal: keep a large reserve for an outage.
  • Changes: autonomy floor on and raised to at least backup_target_soc_percent (80 %) of capacity; its weight is at least backup_shortfall_price_per_kwh (2.0/kWh).
  • Behaviour: refills to ~80 % and avoids discharging below it unless the shortfall is worth more than 2.0/kWh; the floor stays soft, so a plan always exists.
  • Choose when: storm or grid-outage warnings, planned maintenance, cold winter nights. The blueprint's alert rule selects it when your alert entity is on.
  • Watch out: combining it with a low grid-charge ceiling raises grid_charge_ceiling_below_autonomy_weight — the floor could be emptied but never refilled.

pv_swap — PV swap

  • Goal: in low-PV seasons, buy cheap at night and sell the day's real PV output at a later, higher price.
  • Changes: pv_export_margin (0.05/kWh) is subtracted from every sell price (the export must beat the night buy by at least that margin); Sell only PV forced on (daily export ≤ daily PV); grid-charge ceiling forced off (so night charging is not blocked); autonomy floor on.
  • Behaviour: grid-charges overnight, lets the day's PV cover the house, then exports up to the day's generated PV in the evening peak.
  • Choose when: tomorrow's PV forecast is below the daily load and evening sell × round-trip efficiency ≥ night buy + margin (the blueprint's pv_swap rule).
  • Watch out: Sell only PV counts energy, not provenance — exported battery energy is limited in total to the day's PV, not traced to its origin.

max_export — maximum export

  • Goal: pure arbitrage, maximize revenue from exports.
  • Changes: export-benefit hurdle forced to 0, Sell only PV forced off (grid-charged energy can be resold), grid-charge ceiling forced off, autonomy floor off.
  • Behaviour: charges whenever buy is low, discharges into the grid whenever the spread covers losses and wear; may do several export episodes a day.
  • Choose when: exceptional sell prices, a tariff that rewards export.
  • Watch out: most battery cycles; check whether your contract allows reselling grid energy. Never selected automatically.

grid_friendly — grid friendly

  • Goal: flatten the grid profile — avoid high import peaks and limit export power.
  • Changes: peak import term peak_import_price_per_kw (0.50/kW of the highest import power); soft import/export caps grid_friendly_import_cap_kw / grid_friendly_export_cap_kw (0 = site limit), each kWh above them costs cap_violation_price_per_kwh (2.0); autonomy floor off.
  • Behaviour: spreads grid charging over longer windows, uses the battery to shave import peaks, keeps export under the cap.
  • Choose when: capacity/power-based tariffs, a weak connection or a fuse near its limit.
  • Watch out: caps are soft; excess is reported in cap_violation_kwh instead of failing. Never selected automatically.

Plan attributes for strategies

Attribute Meaning
strategy Strategy that produced this plan (may lag the select while a recalculation runs).
autonomy_shortfall_kwh Total shortfall below the autonomy floor; 0 = floor met.
peak_reserve_shortfall_kwh Total shortfall below the peak-period reserve, the entry buffer and the buffer under an export together; 0 = met or off.
time_limited true when the base solve hit solve_time_limit_s and the best validated solution found so far was published instead of a proven optimum.
mip_gap Relative MIP gap the solver reported for the published plan: 0 = proven optimal (a proven plan normally reads 0, or at most 0.0001 when no episode hurdle is active; not a hard bound: HiGHS also stops on its absolute gap of 1e-6, which cannot be switched off, so when the weighted objective the solver minimises is within about ±0.01 of zero the relative gap can be larger, up to roughly 1e-6 / |objective|, which exceeds 1 once the objective is within 1e-6 of zero; that objective is the plan's cost plus the episode reserves and the strategy's penalty terms, so it can be near zero while the plan's cost is not, and the reverse; time_limited, not mip_gap == 0, tells a proven plan from an unproven one); for a time-limited plan, the bound on how far the solver's weighted objective may be from the optimum (e.g. 0.017 = 1.7 %). It does not bound the plan's cost in currency, and the plan itself can differ from the proven one in many intervals (see docs/runtime-validation.md).
cap_violation_kwh Total energy above grid_friendly soft caps; 0 = caps met.

Strategy-switch release

A strategy change is a reset: the carried mode commitment is released so the new strategy is not trapped in the old mode's minimum duration. A current export episode is kept so its hurdle is not charged twice.

Automatic strategy switching

The optional blueprint strategy_switch.yaml picks one strategy per day. It runs at 14:05 (after RCE next-day prices and Solcast), retries hourly until 20:00 if next-day prices are missing, and reconciles a half-applied write at Home Assistant start.

Input Default
Night window 22:00–06:00 (lowest buy price in plan intervals)
Max buy highest buy price across all plan intervals
Evening window 17:00–21:00 (max sell price from RCE next day)
Round-trip efficiency 0.90
Self-sufficiency spread margin 0.15 PLN/kWh
PV swap margin 0.05 PLN/kWh
Enabled rules alert, pv_swap, self_sufficiency (cost_min is the fallback)

A manual change of the select blocks the economic rules until the next successful scheduled run; the alert rule is never blocked. max_export and grid_friendly are manual-only. Setup details: installation guide.

Window notifications

Energy Compass tells the household when extra use is cheap (a favorable window) or when an expensive LIMIT window is starting. It sends notifications only when you turn them on: Notify enabled in Options → Notification preferences is the master switch, and the notification targets say where the messages go. Setup: installation guide.

Turning them on

  1. Open Options → Notification preferences, select at least one target and turn on Notify enabled. Energy Compass sends from the next published plan on.
  2. Run energy_compass.send_test_notification in Developer tools → Actions and check the device.
Setting Meaning
notify_enabled (Notify enabled) the master switch, off by default. On without a target the integration sends nothing, and an installed notification blueprint keeps working as before (see Migrating from the blueprint)
notify_services (Notification services (mobile app)) legacy notify service names without the domain, for example mobile_app_pixel_8. Each is called as notify.<name> with a title and a message. The Home Assistant mobile app still registers this kind
notify_entities (Notification entities) notify entity ids, for example notify.kitchen_display. Each is called with notify.send_message
notify_language (Notification language) auto (default) follows the Home Assistant language: Polish when it starts with pl, otherwise English; en and pl fix it
notify_events favorable, limit or both
notify_minimum_hours minimum time left in a favorable window (default 2 h)
notify_limit_lead_minutes how far ahead a LIMIT window is announced (default 30 min)
quiet_start, quiet_end quiet hours in the Home Assistant time zone (default 22:00–08:00); equal times mean no quiet hours
notify_cooldown_minutes minimum time between two attempts (default 60 min)
notify_daily_max notifications per local day (default 3)

With Notify enabled on, the first target you save makes Energy Compass the sender. A target is one entry of either list. The integration calls every target at once; a target that fails, or does not answer within 30 seconds, does not stop the others. Clearing the targets stops the notifications immediately.

How a notification is decided

The integration looks at the published plan on every plan update and once a minute.

  • When both a LIMIT and a favorable window qualify, LIMIT wins.
  • A window that overlaps the stored one is the same window: recalculations and BOOST/CHEAP changes extend it instead of notifying again, so a new message needs a window that does not overlap.
  • The window, the day's count and the attempt time are saved before the call, so a restart or an options reload never repeats a message and a crash at the wrong moment loses at most one. The store survives restarts; a store that cannot be read starts fresh.
  • Just before the call the gates, the sender, the target, the quiet hours and the plan are checked again; a new plan published in between stops the call (the window stays spent).
  • The cap and the cooldown count attempts, including failed ones. A failed attempt is not retried for the same window.
  • Each message is also written to the logbook on the Plan sensor.
Message When
Use the cheap energy / Wykorzystaj tanią energię a favorable window is running and the whole rest of it is BOOST
A good time for household appliances / Dobry moment na domowe urządzenia a favorable window is running, not all BOOST
Plan heavy use for later / Zaplanuj większe zużycie na później a LIMIT window starts within the lead time, or is already running
Grid outage: the house runs on the battery / Awaria sieci: dom działa na baterii the Deye controller declared a grid outage
Grid is back / Sieć wróciła that outage ended
Energy Compass test / Test Energy Compass only the test action

The message names the window's local times (HH:MM–HH:MM, or dd.mm HH:MM–dd.mm HH:MM when the window crosses midnight) and suggests moving laundry, the dishwasher or car charging.

Inverter clock message

With the Deye controller on, the same sender tells you once per episode when the inverter clock is off ("Deye inverter clock is off": the skew in minutes, plus when the inverter is ahead, and where to set the time). An episode starts when the alert of the Inverter clock turns on and ends when the skew is back under the threshold; a reload of the entry in the middle of one does not send it again. It uses the same targets, language and opt-in as window messages and waits for the end of the quiet hours, but it neither counts against the daily cap nor starts the cooldown, and it is sent while the optimizer alert is on.

Outage messages

With the Deye controller on, the same sender tells you when a grid outage starts and when it ends. It needs only that Notify enabled is on and a target is set (the integration is the sender): quiet hours, the daily cap and the cooldown do not hold it back and it does not count against them, and the optimizer alert does not matter. The text follows Notification language:

Message Text
start, with runtime Grid lost at 14:05. Battery 82 %, about 6 h 10 min at the current 1.2 kW.
start, load unknown or too low Grid lost at 14:05. Battery 82 %.
start, battery unknown Grid lost at 14:05.
end Grid back at 14:40 after 35 min. Battery 79 %.

The runtime is the usable energy above 10 % (the inverter keeps that much) at the load of the plan's current interval; it is left out when the load is under 0.05 kW or the battery capacity or SOC is unknown. The time is the first absent reading (not the end of the debounce), and the end message uses the moment the grid came back, not the end of the stable wait. The start is told once per outage, remembered in the store so a restart does not repeat it, and the end only when the start was told: an outage that began while no target was set stays silent. A start that found no target is not spent, so it is sent when you add one during the outage.

Test action

energy_compass.send_test_notification sends one fixed message to every target of an entry now. It ignores the gates, the quiet hours, the cooldown, the daily cap and the stored window, and it does not change them. The answer lists results: one target, ok and error per target.

Field Meaning
config_entry_id the Energy Compass entry; needed only when more than one is loaded

The action refuses when no target is selected. A test that reaches every target also clears the failure count below.

Notification preferences attribute

The Plan sensor publishes notification_preferences, and that is what decides who sends.

Key Meaning
notify_events, notify_minimum_hours, notify_limit_lead_minutes, notify_cooldown_minutes, notify_daily_max, quiet_start, quiet_end the settings above as the plan was computed with them
notify_sender who sends: "integration" when Notify enabled is on and a target is set, "blueprint" when it is on without a target, "off" when it is off
notify_enabled not the setting: it means "the blueprint may send". It is true only while notify_sender is "blueprint", so the deprecated blueprint, which sends only while it is true, goes silent as soon as the integration is the sender
actions_configured a saved legacy action list exists; the native sender does not use it

After you save options, the sender changes with the next published plan, not before. While an old plan is retained, the blueprint keeps sending until the new plan arrives and the integration waits for it, so the two never send together.

Repair issues

Issue When What to do
notify_send_failed three attempts in a row reached no target or only some of them; the text names the targets and the last error fix the target in Notification preferences and run the test action. It clears after the next successful notification or test, and starts over when you change the targets
notify_blueprint_deprecated an automation made from the notification blueprint is on while Notify enabled is on and the blueprint is still the sender follow Migrating from the blueprint
notify_blueprint_suppressed the same automation is on but the integration now sends, so the automation sends nothing delete the automation and its five helpers

Migrating from the blueprint

  1. Update Energy Compass. Nothing changes yet: with no target selected the blueprint keeps sending, and a repair issue says it is deprecated.
  2. In Options → Notification preferences select your phone's mobile_app_… service (the one the blueprint's action called) or a notify entity. Save.
  3. Set Notification language if the blueprint's language differed from Home Assistant's.
  4. Run energy_compass.send_test_notification in Developer tools → Actions and check the phone.
  5. From the next plan on, Energy Compass sends and the blueprint goes silent. The repair issue now says the automation is suppressed.
  6. Delete the automation and the five helpers (two Text, one Number, two Date/time).

The integration starts with no remembered window. A favorable or LIMIT window that is running at the moment of the switch and that the blueprint already announced may be announced once more. This happens at most once per running window, and only within the cap and the cooldown, which also start fresh. Blueprint overrides (use_blueprint_overrides) have no native counterpart: copy their values into Notification preferences before step 2.

Blueprint (deprecated)

The optional blueprint notifications.yaml is deprecated and will be removed in a later release. It still works while the integration is not the sender; once the integration sends it is silent, because it sends only while the plan's notification_preferences.notify_enabled is true. Setup: installation guide.

The action receives notification_title, notification_message and event_kind.

Input Meaning
compass, plan, forecast_valid, alert, optimizer_status Consumption compass, Plan, Forecast valid, Alert and Optimizer status of one installation
next_boost, next_cheap, next_limit the three window start sensors (their changes re-run the automation)
last_favorable, last_limit Text helpers (max 255) holding the last window as {"s": start, "e": end}
daily_count, daily_date, last_sent Number helper and two Date/time helpers for the daily cap and cooldown
language en or pl for the title and message
use_blueprint_overrides off: use the integration's notification preferences; on: use the inputs below
enabled_events, minimum_hours, limit_lead_minutes, quiet_start, quiet_end, cooldown_minutes, daily_cap overrides: events, minimum favorable time remaining, LIMIT lead, quiet hours, cooldown, messages per local day
notification_actions the action to run, for example a mobile app notify action

Cost card

The optional card custom:energy-compass-cost-card (cards/cost/) shows the purchase cost of grid energy, the value of exported energy (the prosumer deposit in Polish net-billing) and the balance purchase − deposit: today measured and planned to midnight, and month and year from statistics. Install and full description: cost card guide.

Key Meaning
cost_entity, import_entity, export_entity purchase cost (statistics), grid import and export energy (kWh) — required
plan_entity, valid_entity, export_prices_entity Plan, Forecast valid and the export price forecast (prices) — required
import_price_entity buy price used to fill a purchase-cost gap after a restart
deposit_entity, deposit_backfill export value sensor and the backfilled history statistic, for month and year
runtime_entity, mode_entity Deye controller runtime and mode, to say whether the plan is executed
currency, language, tariff_label, footnote presentation

The month and year deposit comes from the export value counter blueprint: it adds every increase of the export meter (export_energy), valued at the price forecast (export_prices), to a Number helper (counter); jumps above max_step_kwh are ignored.

Deye inverter controller (Solarman)

Energy Compass is advisory by default and writes to an inverter only when you enable the optional Deye controller (Options → Deye controller, off by default). The controller executes the plan on a Deye hybrid inverter through the Solarman integration: it writes three battery currents and the six time-of-use (TOU) programs, and reads every write back from the holding registers. With the native engine it runs inside the integration: no blueprint, automation, package, helper or configuration.yaml edit is needed, the accepted plan survives an entry reload, and Energy Compass owns the mode, the accepted plan, the session and the revocation, the timing of the next run and the stored runtime. It needs Energy Compass 0.1.38 or newer. Setup steps are in the installation guide. The deye_hybrid setup profile pre-fills idle_drain_kw 0.13 and refresh_minutes 60 for a new installation; see Setup profiles.

The earlier executor, the blueprint deye_solarman_controller.yaml, is deprecated. It still works in this release as the blueprint engine (the value of every entry created before 0.1.38) and is removed in the release after next, together with its generator tools/deye_controller/build.py, the energy_compass.controller_runtime and energy_compass.controller_import_package services and the sections below that describe it. Move to the native engine as described in Migrating from the blueprint.

Enabling the controller

Open Options → Deye controller, switch Enable the Deye controller on and choose the Solarman inverter device (it is preselected when there is only one). Energy Compass finds the six TOU programs (time, power, voltage, SOC and charging, 30 entities) on that device by the Solarman translation keys program_1_time … program_6_charging, derives the entity ID prefix they share and tracks them. It refuses the device when a program is missing or disabled, when the entity IDs do not share one prefix, or when another Energy Compass entry already controls it. Enabling reloads the entry once; moving the controller to another device applies live. Both are refused while the mode is not Off or a restore is pending: select Off and wait until restore_pending is off first, otherwise nothing could restore the base profile. The step is visible without the expert toggle.

Engine. The step has an Engine field. native (the default for a new enable) lets Energy Compass execute the plan itself and write the inverter through the Solarman entities and the solarman.read_holding_registers service; no blueprint or automation is needed. blueprint (deprecated; the value of every entry created before 0.1.38) keeps the Deye controller blueprint as the executor. Changing the engine reloads the entry and is refused while the mode is not Off or a restore is pending. The native engine finds the battery currents, operation mode, SOC, voltage and discharge counter on the same device by the Solarman keys battery_max_charging_current, battery_max_discharging_current, battery_grid_charging_current, battery_operation_mode, battery, battery_voltage and total_battery_discharge, and names what is missing. Only high-voltage packs (400–610 V) are supported: a pack measured below 400 V is refused.

Limits and takeover (expert settings). The maximum battery power defaults to the smaller of the charge and discharge power in the Energy Compass settings; the currents default to the entity's own maximum, capped at that power divided by 400 V. Hold, reached-discharge and balance currents, the grid-charge voltage ceiling, the commissioned battery modes, the previous automations to wait for, the telemetry entities, the discharge counter and an override for each entity can be set; an empty field keeps its default. Limits apply on the next run without a reload. When one blueprint automation exists, its inputs are loaded into these fields for you to review before saving.

Do not enable the controller on a net-metering installation: the right plan there is the inverter's own self-use mode (see Setup profiles).

An installation that ran the 0.1.36 package, has one Energy Compass entry and exactly one Solarman device with all six programs gets the controller enabled automatically at the first start of 0.1.37. The mode starts at Off, so nothing is written until you choose one; see Migrating from the package.

Supported hardware

What Verified
Inverter Deye SG0*HP3 three-phase high-voltage hybrid inverters; the Solarman device sensor reports the type "HV 3-Phase Hybrid Inverter"
Protocol version 1.4 (attribute Protocol Version of that sensor)
Battery pack high-voltage lithium (LFP) pack, 400–610 V
Integration ha-solarman 25.08.16; the entities are found by their translation keys and the registers are read with solarman.read_holding_registers
48 V (low-voltage) Deye models not supported yet: the options step refuses to enable the native engine below 400 V, and a run outside 400–610 V writes nothing

The tested unit is a SG0*HP3 with control board firmware 3002-1095-11408. Firmware versions are recorded in the hardware attribute but not compared: nothing is known about per-firmware differences. A device whose type and protocol are not on the list is not blocked. It raises the repair issue "Deye inverter not verified" (a dismissible warning) and sets hardware.verified to false; use Simulation first, as for every installation.

Layout probe. Before the first write that forces a profile in a session, the native engine reads registers 108–177 and compares them with the states of the 27 entities it writes (the three currents and the 24 TOU values). Numbers and selects must agree; a select whose register holds a value outside the known map (Disabled, Grid, Sell) says nothing about the layout and is skipped, because the controller rewrites it anyway. Any other difference, a missing register or an unavailable entity stops the run with the runtime code blocked and the reason layout_mismatch, which lists the entities; nothing is written and the check repeats on the next run, because entities can lag one Solarman poll behind a manual change. The probe also runs in Simulation, so a wrong layout shows before Auto. A passed probe holds for the session, the device and the set of entities read: a changed device or an entity override probes again. Restoring the base profile does not wait for the probe, because it writes through Solarman's own entities and only the read-back depends on the layout; forcing a profile does.

Inverter clock

The inverter runs its TOU programs by its own clock, but Energy Compass writes them by Home Assistant local time. A clock that disagrees moves every window: on the live site the inverter stayed on summer time after the change to winter time and then drifted slow, so it was 49 minutes ahead, switched to the next program 49 minutes early and never did the grid charge the controller had written, while every write was confirmed and the runtime code was ok. The controller therefore compares the clocks and tells you. It only tells you: it changes no write and no plan because of the skew.

  • Source. The Solarman date and time entity of the chosen device (datetime.<prefix>date_time, found by the device like the program entities). A device without it is not checked, silently.
  • Skew is the inverter clock minus Home Assistant time, both read in the Home Assistant time zone; plus means the inverter is ahead. A change between summer and winter time that the inverter did not follow shows as ±60 minutes.
  • Threshold. More than 5 minutes (|skew| > 5 min), held for 10 minutes of fresh readings, so one bad read does not alert. A reading under the threshold starts the hold over; an unreadable or older than 5 minutes state changes nothing (nothing is raised and nothing is cleared).
  • Reaction while it holds:
  • tou_problem on the controller sensor is inverter_clock_skew (a resolution failure keeps its own code) and the attribute clock shows clock_skew_seconds, clock_skew_minutes, inverter_clock, clock_read_at, over_threshold_since and alert;
  • the repair issue "Deye inverter clock is off by N min" (a warning, not fixable) gives the skew, the two times, the likely cause and the fix;
  • Alert turns on with code inverter_clock_skew, reason the skew and clock_skew_minutes;
  • with the native notifications on, one message per episode is sent.
  • Recovery. A reading back under the threshold clears the issue, the tou_problem and the alert, and ends the episode. The diagnostics (deye_controller.clock) carry the same fields, also while no alert is on.

TOU windows run at wrong times. Look at the Deye controller sensor first: tou_problem = inverter_clock_skew and the repair issue mean the inverter clock is off, not the plan. Typical causes are a change between summer and winter time that the inverter did not follow and drift on a logger that has no cloud time sync (the Solarman cloud entity of the logger is unavailable). Energy Compass cannot set the clock: this inverter accepts writes to the clock registers (0x003E–0x0040) over Modbus and ignores them. Set the date and time on the inverter panel or in the Deye app; the alert clears about a minute after the corrected clock is read, or within the poll interval. If tou_problem is empty and the windows are still off, compare the tou attribute with the program entities of the device.

Controller entities

Four entities exist only while the controller is enabled, a fifth with the native engine; they sit on the Energy Compass device. <name> is the entry title.

Key Entity Role
deye_controller sensor.<name>_deye_controller (timestamp) the state is the next instant the executor must run (the earliest row end, valid_until, coverage_end or TOU program boundary); the attributes are the contract below
deye_mode select.<name>_deye_mode Off / Simulation / Auto; the only switch you operate; the options are not translated
deye_runtime sensor.<name>_deye_controller_runtime runtime code (below); attribute runtime holds state, reason, confirmed values and uncertain registers
deye_pause switch.<name>_pause_inverter_writes Pause inverter writes; only with the native engine. While on, the controller computes and publishes the decision but sends no write; restore_pending and the uncertain registers stay as they are and the runtime code is paused. A run in flight stops before its next write; turning the switch off requests a run. Mode Off keeps its meaning: with nothing to restore the run reports released even when paused, and with a restore pending the pause wins and the restore waits. The flag is saved at once, survives a reload and is cleared when the engine is switched to blueprint
grid_outage binary_sensor.<name>_grid_outage (problem) Grid outage; either engine. On while the grid is out (Grid outage); unavailable until a presence entity or a phase voltage is read. Attributes: since (when the outage was declared), lost_at (the first absent reading, kept after the outage), restored_pending_since (the grid is back and the stable-presence wait has begun), source (entity or voltage) and source_state (what that source reported)

The IDs depend on the entry name and the language the entities were created in (a Polish instance gets names such as …_sterownik_deye); read them from the device page. The blueprint engine needs only the controller sensor; it finds the mode entity and the TOU prefix through its attributes.

Controller attribute Meaning
controller_schema 1; the blueprint refuses a controller with another schema
mode, mode_entity the mode (mirrored from the select, so a change runs the blueprint) and the select's entity ID
restore_pending on from the first write until the base profile is confirmed again
session session stamp of this Home Assistant run (a float timestamp)
plan_reason whether the accepted plan may be executed: ok, session, revoked, grid_outage or sources (below)
status optimizer status of the latest publication
retained the latest publication is a retained plan (status calculating)
generation, valid_until, coverage_end, accepted_at the accepted plan: generated_at, original deadline, end of the last interval and acceptance time
revoked_generation, revoked_at, revoked_reason the last revocation
capacity_kwh, eta_charge, eta_discharge, charge_kw, discharge_kw battery parameters of the accepted generation (current settings while nothing is accepted)
device_id, program_prefix, tou_problem the chosen Solarman device, the TOU entity prefix and what is wrong: why resolution failed (tou_incomplete, tou_prefix) or inverter_clock_skew (see Inverter clock)
next_tou next local TOU program boundary
accepted the accepted plan snapshot (rows, dispatch policy, battery); not recorded
tou state of the 30 TOU entities; a change re-runs the blueprint; not recorded
clock the inverter clock check (Inverter clock): clock_skew_seconds, clock_skew_minutes, inverter_clock, clock_read_at, over_threshold_since and alert; empty (null) when the device has no date and time entity
grid the grid watch (Grid outage): source, raw, present, active, since, lost_at, off_since, on_since and restored_at; empty (null) when neither a presence entity nor a phase voltage is found
hardware the inverter as the Solarman device sensor reports it: device type, protocol, control and communication board firmware, rated power, registry model and verified (the type and protocol pair is on the tested list); no serial number

The runtime sensor carries the recorded attributes restore_pending, reason, state, requested_mode, confirmed_mode, since, warning, takeover_blocked and accepted_generation, plus runtime and updated_at, which are not recorded. It is written at once when its code or one of the recorded attributes changes and at most once a minute for other changes. Acceptances, revocations, session drops, mode changes, imports and device changes go to a history of 50 entries in the store and in the integration's diagnostics (deye_controller); no events are fired.

With the native engine the runtime sensor also has last_run (not recorded): what triggered the last run, the decision, the planned commands, each write with its outcome (sent, failed, confirmed or blocked), the register layout probe result when one ran (probe: passed or failed: <entities>) and how the run ended. The last 50 runs are kept in memory, not in the store, and appear in the diagnostics as run_history; the last 20 runs that sent a command or ended with a runtime code other than ok are kept separately as run_history_notable, so routine runs cannot push them out. The engine runs when something it reads changes (a plan, the mode, a pause, the TOU facts, the next row or TOU boundary), on each full minute and when an inverter value changes; it does not run on every refresh of Energy Compass. A logbook entry names the old and new runtime code and confirmed mode whenever either changes.

Services

Service Purpose
energy_compass.controller_runtime reads or replaces the stored runtime and the restore flag and answers with runtime, restore_pending and session. Used by the blueprint; unknown keys, non-objects and more than 32 768 bytes are rejected
energy_compass.controller_import_package administrator only; one-time copy of mode, session, accepted plan and runtime from the 0.1.36 package (see Migrating); refuses with package_import_refused once it has run, even before the new blueprint writes, unless force is set

Modes

Auto writes; Simulation computes every target and records it in runtime without touching the inverter; Off releases control. Leaving Auto for Off restores the base profile once, confirms it, then leaves later manual settings alone. Disabling the automation skips that restore. A switch to Simulation while a restore is pending is refused: the mode goes to Off, the base profile is restored, and Simulation can then be chosen again.

Plan acceptance

Energy Compass accepts a plan inside the callback that publishes it, so the plan, status, validity and alert are one atomic view and there is no split publication. A publication is accepted only when all of these hold: its intervals are contiguous, every row has a known state, a boolean balance_hold and finite non-negative energies (prices may be negative), and one row covers now; the dispatch policy is present; it was generated after the session start and no later than now, it is newer than the accepted plan and it was generated after the last revocation; Forecast valid is on; there is no Alert; the status is ready with no refresh or retention in progress, or calculating while retaining a complete plan; and valid_until is in the future. The mode does not matter: acceptance runs in Off and Simulation too.

An optimizer status other than ready/calculating or an Alert revokes the accepted plan at the time of the publication, so a plan computed before the revocation is never accepted. While the error persists, each publication revokes again but keeps the time of the first revocation of that plan. An entry unload or reload is not an error: the accepted plan is kept in the integration's store and executes while Energy Compass recalculates. After a Home Assistant restart the controller stays on the base profile until the first plan of the new session, because a plan accepted in an earlier run is dropped when the session changes. Saving the integration options does not reload the entry in most cases (Saving options), and when it does, the accepted plan is kept.

plan_reason summarizes the verdict; the blueprint maps it to its (Polish) reasons in this order:

plan_reason Meaning
session nothing is accepted in this session yet (after a restart or before the first plan)
revoked the accepted generation was revoked after an error; a new plan is required
grid_outage the grid is out (native engine only): the accepted plan is still good, and the controller runs BACKUP instead of it until the grid has been back for the stable time
sources an Alert is on, or the latest publication is neither a retained plan nor the accepted ready plan
ok the accepted plan may be executed

Control also requires fresh telemetry: every entity in telemetry_entities numeric and reported within 30 s, battery voltage 400–610 V and SOC 0–100 %. Every automation in old_writers must be off and not running. A snapshot without battery parameters blocks control with the reason plan: brak parametrów baterii (pojemność, sprawność) w planie.

Profiles

A battery current is never written as 0 A: a charge or discharge current the table lists as 0 A is written as min_buffer_current (1 A by default; 0 is the expert opt-out, see Limits and defaults), so the battery stays connected as the buffer of the house. The base profile writes relinquish_current instead. The grid charge current is not a battery limit and stays 0 A.

Plan state Charge / discharge current Grid charge current TOU direction, target
CHARGE_PV, SELF_CONSUME cap / cap 0 A all Disabled, SOC 10 %
CURTAIL with charge_kwh above 0.000001 kWh planned, from hold_grid_current to the cap / 0 A 0 A all Disabled, SOC 10 %
HOLD, CHARGE_PV, SELF_CONSUME and a charging CURTAIL at SOC ≥ 100 % in Voltage mode (HOLD: kept until SOC ≤ 99 %) cap / cap in CHARGE_PV and SELF_CONSUME, cap / discharge cap in HOLD and CURTAIL 0 A all Disabled, SOC 10 %
CHARGE_GRID cap / cap planned grid share, ≤ max_grid_current Grid on the active program, target SOC from the plan; in Voltage mode TOU voltage voltage_grid_charge_ceiling
DISCHARGE_GRID 0 A / planned, ≤ cap; after the target is reached reached_discharge_current, ≤ cap 0 A Sell on the active program, target SOC from the plan, power = planned, ≤ max_power_w; Disabled after the target is reached
HOLD, CURTAIL with charge_kwh up to 0.000001 kWh the larger of hold_grid_current and min_buffer_current / discharge cap 0 A Grid, target SOC = the lower of the planned end SOC (rounded down) and the live level, latched (below)
BACKUP (grid outage, native engine) cap / cap 0 A all Disabled, SOC 10 %, 49.6 (496 V), power max_power_w
base (release, invalid plan) relinquish_current / relinquish_current 0 A all Disabled, SOC 10 %, 49.6 (496 V), power max_power_w

The cap is min(max_current, max_power_w / V) for charging and min(max_current, max_power_w × eta_discharge / V) for discharging. The cap has hysteresis: the current already on the inverter is kept while it still fits the power cap, and the next ampere step is taken only with 2 % voltage headroom (about 10 V at 530 V), so a pack voltage crossing a step boundary does not rewrite the ceiling on every sag and rebound. The power cap is never exceeded. At 100 % SOC the charge current of CHARGE_PV, SELF_CONSUME and CHARGE_GRID becomes 0 A; in battery operation mode Voltage only CHARGE_GRID does, because the other two follow the full-pack rule at the end of this paragraph. Planned currents convert interval kWh with eta_charge (charging) or eta_discharge (discharging) over the full interval. Target SOC uses the accepted plan's capacity_kwh; target voltage follows a fixed high-voltage LFP curve (496–536 V for 10–90 %, 584 V charging or 544 V discharging at 100 %). A reached target in CHARGE_GRID/DISCHARGE_GRID is latched for that plan interval. A reached DISCHARGE_GRID interval switches the direction to Disabled but keeps reached_discharge_current (1 A, about 530 W at 530 V, never above the cap) on discharge, so the battery covers the house base load without selling and larger loads come from the grid; 0 A would send the whole house load to the grid at a full battery. An interval whose planned discharge_kwh is below the 0.05 kWh tolerance (export planned from PV) is reached at once. In an LFP balance row (balance_hold: true) the charge current stays on at 100 %, CHARGE_GRID targets 100 % and the grid current is at least balance_grid_current. In Voltage mode the inverter ends charging on pack voltage, and a counter-based SOC source can read 100 % before the pack is full. So at SOC ≥ 100 % in HOLD, CHARGE_PV and SELF_CONSUME the controller keeps the normal charge current cap (with the same hysteresis, so there are no 0 A rewrites around the ceiling) instead of the buffer current. The grid current is 0 A, so PV is the only source, discharge is the cap in HOLD, and no SOC target is written and no "reached" state is latched. In HOLD the switch has hysteresis: the full-pack profile starts at SOC ≥ 100 % and stays through the following HOLD runs until SOC is 99 % or lower, so an SOC source that dithers between 99.9 % and 100 % does not rewrite the profile on every crossing. Each switch is one write transaction that begins with charge 0 A, and there is at most one per percentage point of SOC movement; without PV the pack drifts down on the inverter's own draw and HOLD holds it at the level it is at, a cycle of hours. CHARGE_PV and SELF_CONSUME need no hysteresis, because below 100 % they write the same values. CHARGE_GRID (it keeps voltage_grid_charge_ceiling and its 0 A charge current at 100 %), the balance hold and Capacity mode behave as before. A CURTAIL row that charges (charge_kwh above 0.000001 kWh: the PV above what the site passes is more than the pack takes at the charge power) runs like CHARGE_PV without discharge, at the planned current: the charge current is charge_kwh × eta_charge / (h × V) rounded up to the step of the charge entity, at least hold_grid_current and at most the cap, the grid current 0 A, the discharge current 0 A, all programs Disabled, so the pack takes PV at that current and the inverter curtails the rest by itself. A row that plans the charge power over its whole interval gets the whole cap. A row that plans less (the charge of such a row is free between zero and the PV left after the curtailment and the house, and the plan took less) charges less than the cap would, so the pack ends where the plan says and not above it.
